A singular value decomposition approach may also be used to deal with the matrix inversion issue; see [BeT96], Section 3.2.2. 
Thus a linear architecture has the important advantage that the training problem can be solved exactly and conveniently with the formula (4.7) (of course it may be solved by any other algorithm that is suitable for linear least squares problems, including iterative algorithms). By contrast, if we use a nonlinear architecture, such as a neural network, the associated least squares problem is nonquadratic and also nonconvex, so it is hard to solve in principle. Despite this fact, through a combination of sophisticated implementation of special gradient algorithms, called incremental , and powerful computational resources, neural network methods have been successful in practice. 
Incremental Gradient Methods 
We will now discuss briefly special methods for solution of the nonlinear least squares training problem (4.6), assuming a parametric architecture that is di!erentiable in the parameter vector. This methodology can be properly viewed as a subject in nonlinear programming and iterative algorithms, and as such it can be studied independently of the approximate DP methods of this book. Thus the reader who has already some exposure to the subject may skip to the next section. The nonlinear programming textbook [Ber16] and the RL book [Ber19a] provide more detailed presentations.

Thus a single component function fik is used at iteration k, with great economies in gradient calculation cost over the ordinary gradient method (4.9), particularly when m is large. The idea is to attain faster convergence when far from the solution; see the books [BeT96] and [Ber19a] for a more detailed discussion of this point. 
The method for selecting the index ik of the component to be iterated on at iteration k is important for the performance of the method. We describe three common rules , the last two of which involve randomization:‡ 
(1) A cyclic order , the simplest rule, whereby the indexes are taken up in the fixed deterministic order 1, . . . ,m, so that ik is equal to (k modulo m) plus 1. A contiguous block of iterations involving the components f1, . . . , fm in this order and exactly once is called a cycle. 
(2) A uniform random order , whereby the index ik chosen randomly by sampling over all indexes with a uniform distribution, independently of the past history of the algorithm. This rule may perform better than the cyclic rule in some circumstances.

Note that in the cyclic cases, it is essential to include all components in a cycle; otherwise some components will be sampled more often than others, leading to a bias in the convergence process. Similarly, it is necessary to sample according to the uniform distribution in the random order case. 
The choice of the stepsize %k plays an important role in the performance of incremental gradient methods. In practice, it is common to use a constant stepsize for a (possibly prespecified) number of iterations, then decrease the stepsize by a certain factor, and repeat, up to the point where the stepsize reaches a prespecified floor value. An alternative possibility is to use a diminishing stepsize rule of the form

where %, $1, and $2 are some positive scalars. There are also variants of the method that use a constant stepsize throughout, and can be shown to converge to a stationary point of f under reasonable assumptions. In one type of such method the degree of incrementalism gradually diminishes as the method progresses (see [Ber97a]). Another incremental approach with similar aims, is the aggregated gradient method, which is discussed in the author’s textbooks [Ber15a], [Ber16], [Ber19a]. 
Regardless of whether a constant or a diminishing stepsize is ultimately used, the incremental method must use a much larger stepsize than the corresponding nonincremental gradient method (as much as m times larger, so that the size of the incremental gradient step is comparable to the size of the nonincremental gradient step). 
One possibility is to use an adaptive stepsize rule, whereby, roughly speaking, the stepsize is reduced (or increased) when the progress of the method indicates that the algorithm is (or is not) oscillating. There are formal ways to implement such stepsize rules with sound convergence properties (see [Tse98], [MYF03]). 
The di#culty with stepsize selection may also be addressed with diagonal scaling, i.e., using a stepsize %k

The RL book [Ber19a] (Section 3.1.3) describes another type method that involves second derivatives and is based on Newton’s method. The idea here is to write Newton’s method in a format that is well suited to the additive character of the cost function f , and involves low order matrix inversion. One can then implement diagonal scaling by setting to zero the o!-diagonal terms of the inverted matrices, so that the algorithm involves no matrix inversion. There is also another related algorithm, which is based on the Gauss-Newton method and the extended Kalman filter; see the paper [Ber96] and the book [BeT96], Section 3.2.6. 
4.2 NEURAL NETWORKS 
There are several di!erent types of neural networks that can be used for a variety of tasks, such as pattern recognition, classification, image and speech recognition, and others. In this section, we focus on our finite horizon DP context, and the role that neural networks can play in approximating the optimal cost-to-go functions J*

Note that each value ""(x, v) depends on just the #th row of A and the #th component of b, not on the entire vector v. In some cases this motivates placing some constraints on individual components of A and b to achieve special problem-dependent “handcrafted” e!ects. 
State Encoding and Direct Feature Extraction 
The state encoding operation that transforms x into the neural network input y(x) can be instrumental in the success of the approximation scheme. Examples of state encodings are components of the state x, numerical representations of qualitative characteristics of x, and more generally features of x, i.e., functions of x that aim to capture “important nonlinearities” of the optimal cost-to-go function. With the latter view of state encoding, we may consider the approximation process as consisting of a feature extraction mapping, followed by a neural network with input the extracted features of x, and output the cost-to-go approximation; see Fig. 4.2.4. 
The idea here is that with a good feature extraction mapping, the neural network need not be very complicated (may involve few nonlinear units and corresponding parameters), and may be trained more easily. This intuition is borne out by simple examples and practical experience. How-ever, as is often the case with neural networks, it is hard to support it with a quantitative analysis. 
Universal Approximation Property of Neural Networks 
An important question is how well we can approximate the target function J* k with a neural network architecture, assuming we can choose the num-
ber of the nonlinear units m to be as large as we want. The answer to this question is quite favorable and is provided by the so-called universal approximation theorem.

Roughly, the theorem says that assuming that x is an element of a Euclidean space X and y(x) ' x, a neural network of the form described can approximate arbitrarily closely (in an appropriate mathematical sense), over a compact subset S ( X , any piecewise continuous function J : S )* #, provided the number m of nonlinear units is su#ciently large. For proofs of the theorem, we refer to Cybenko [Cyb89], Funahashi [Fun89], Hornik, Stinchcombe, and White [HSW89], and Leshno et al. [LLP93]. For additional sources and intuitive explanations we refer to Bishop ([Bis95], pp. 129-130), Jones [Jon90], and the RL textbook [Ber19a], Section 3.2.1. 
While the universal approximation theorem provides some assurance about the adequacy of the neural network structure, it does not predict how many nonlinear units we may need for “good” performance in a given problem. Unfortunately, this is a di#cult question to even pose precisely, let alone to answer adequately. In practice, one is often reduced to trying increasingly larger values of m until one is convinced that satisfactory performance has been obtained for the task at hand [more systematic optimization approaches, based on Bayesian optimization (cf. Section 3.5), have also been tried, including for AlphaZero [SHS17]]. Experience has shown that in many cases the number of required nonlinear units and corresponding dimension of A can be very large, adding significantly to the di#culty of solving the training problem. This has given rise to many suggestions for modifications of the neural network structure. One possibility is to concatenate multiple single layer perceptrons so that the output of the nonlinear layer of one perceptron becomes the input to the linear layer of the next, giving rise to deep neural networks, which we will discuss later. 
4.2.1 Training of Neural Networks 
Given a set of state-cost training pairs (xs,$s), s = 1, . . . , q, the parameters of the neural network A, b, and r are obtained by solving the problem

308 Learning Values and Policies Chap. 4 
Note that the cost function of this problem is generally nonconvex, so there may exist multiple local minima. 
In practice it is common to augment the cost function of this problem with a regularization function, such as a quadratic in the parameters A, b, and r. This is customary in least squares problems in order to make the problem easier to solve algorithmically. However, in the context of neural network training, regularization is primarily important for a di!erent reason: it helps to avoid overfitting, which occurs when the number of parameters of the neural network is relatively large (comparable to the size of the training set). In this case a neural network model matches the training data very well but may not do as well on new data. This is a well known di#culty, which is the subject of much current research, particularly in the context of deep neural networks. 
An important issue is to select a method to solve the training problem (4.12). While we can use any unconstrained optimization method that is based on gradients, in practice it is important to take into account the cost function structure of problem (4.12). The salient characteristic of this cost function is that it is the sum of a potentially very large number q of component functions. This makes the computation of the cost function value of the training problem and/or its gradient very costly. For this reason the incremental methods of Section 4.1.3 are universally used for training.† Experience has shown that these methods can be vastly superior to their nonincremental counterparts in the context of neural network training. 
The implementation of the training process has benefited from experience that has been accumulated over time, and has provided guidelines for scaling, regularization, initial parameter selection, and other practical issues; we refer to books on neural networks such as Bishop [Bis95], Goodfellow, Bengio, and Courville [GBC16], and Haykin [Hay08], and to the overview paper on deep neural network training [Sun19] for related accounts. Still, incremental methods can be quite slow, and training may be a time-consuming process. Fortunately, the training is ordinarily done o!-line, possibly using parallel computation, in which case computation time may not be a serious issue. Moreover, in practice the neural network training problem typically need not be solved with great accuracy.

volves a concatenation of multiple layers of linear and nonlinear functions; see Fig. 4.2.5. In particular the outputs of each nonlinear layer become the inputs of the next linear layer. In some cases it may make sense to add as additional inputs some of the components of the state x or the state encoding y(x). 
In the early days of neural networks practitioners tended to use few nonlinear layers (say one to three). However, more recently a lot of success in certain problem domains (including image and speech processing, as well as approximate DP) has been achieved with so called deep neural networks , which involve a considerably larger number of layers. 
There are a few questions to consider here. The first has to do with the reason for having multiple nonlinear layers, when a single one is su#cient to guarantee the universal approximation property. Here are some qualitative (and somewhat speculative) explanations: 
(a) If we view the outputs of each nonlinear layer as features, we see that the multilayer network produces a hierarchy of features, where each set of features is a function of the preceding set of features [except for the first set of features, which is a function of the encoding y(x) of the state x]. In the context of specific applications, this hierarchical structure can be exploited to specialize the role of some of the layers and to enhance some characteristics of the state. 
(b) Given the presence of multiple linear layers, one may consider the possibility of using matrices A with a particular sparsity pattern, or other structure that embodies special linear operations such as convolution, which may be well-matched to the training problem at hand. Moreover, when such structures are used, the training problem often becomes easier, because the number of parameters in the linear layers is drastically decreased. 
(c) Overparametrization (more weights than data, as in a multilayer neural network) may help to mitigate the detrimental e!ects of overfitting, and the attendant need for regularization. The explanation for
310 Learning Values and Policies Chap. 4 
this fascinating phenomenon (observed as early as the late 90s) is the subject of much current research; see [ZBH16], [BMM18], [BRT18], [SJL18], [ADH19], [BLL19], [HMR19], [MVS19], [SuY19], [Sun19], [ZBH21] for representative works. The book by Hardt and Recht [HaR21] provides a nice recent account. 
We finally note that the use of deep neural networks has been an important factor for the success of the AlphaGo and AlphaZero programs that play Go and chess, respectively; see [SHM16], [SHS17]. By contrast, Tesauro’s backgammon program and its descendants (cf. Section 2.4) have performed well with one or two nonlinear layers [PaR12]. 
4.3 TRAINING OF COST FUNCTIONS IN APPROXIMATE DP 
In the context of RL, architectures are mainly used to approximate either cost functions or policies. When a neural network is involved, the terms value network and policy network are commonly used, respectively.† In this section we will illustrate the use of value networks in finite horizon DP, while in the next section we will discuss the use of policy networks. We will also illustrate in Section 4.4.1 the combined use of policy and value networks in perpetual rollout , a form of repeated rollout, whereby the rollout policy and its cost function are approximated by a policy and a value network, respectively, to generate a sequence of (approximately) improved rollout policies; see also Chapter 5. 
4.3.1 Fitted Value Iteration 
Let us describe a popular approach for training an approximation architecture J̃k(xk, rk) for a finite horizon DP problem. The parameter vectors rk are determined sequentially, starting from the end of the horizon, and proceeding backwards as in the DP algorithm: first rN"1 then rN"2, and so on. The algorithm samples the state space for each stage k, and generates a large number of states xs 
k, s = 1, . . . , q. It then determines sequentially the parameter vectors rk to obtain a good “least squares fit” to the DP algorithm. The method also can be used in the infinite horizon case, in essentially identical form, and it is commonly called fitted value iteration. 
In particular, each rk is determined by generating a large number of sample states and solving a least squares problem that aims to minimize the error in satisfying the DP equation for these states at time k. At the typical stage k, having obtained rk+1, we determine rk from the least

An important implementation issue is how to select the sample states xs k, s = 1, . . . , q, k = 0, . . . , N ! 1. In practice, they are typically obtained 
by some form of Monte Carlo simulation, but the distribution by which
312 Learning Values and Policies Chap. 4 
they are generated is important for the success of the method. In particular, it is important that the sample states are “representative” in the sense that they are visited often under a nearly optimal policy. More precisely, the frequencies with which various states appear in the sample should be roughly proportional to the probabilities of their occurrence under an optimal policy. 
Aside from the issue of selection of the sampling distribution that we have just described, a di#culty with fitted value iteration arises when the horizon N is very long, since then the total number of parameters over the N stages may become excessive. In this case, however, the problem is often stationary, in the sense that the system and cost per stage do not change as time progresses. Then it may be possible to treat the problem as one with an infinite horizon and bring to bear additional methods for training approximation architectures; see the relevant discussions in Chapter 5.

Having obtained the weight vectors r0, . . . , rN"1, and hence the onestep lookahead policy !̃ = {µ̃0, . . . , µ̃N"1} through Eq. (4.21), a further possibility is to approximate this policy with a parametric architecture. This is approximation in policy space built on top of approximation in value space; see the discussion of Section 2.1.3. The idea here is to simplify even further the on-line computation of the suboptimal controls by avoiding the minimization of Eq. (4.21).

Note that in the absence of approximations, selecting controls by advantage updating is clearly equivalent to selecting controls by comparing their Q-factors. By contrast, when approximation is involved, comparing advantages instead of Q-factors can be important, because the former may have a much smaller range of values than the latter. In particular, Q*

4.4.1 The Use of Classifiers for Approximation in Policy Space 
As we have noted in Section 4.1, in the case of a continuous control space, training of a parametric architecture for policy approximation is similar to training for a cost approximation. In the case where the control space is finite, however, it is useful to make the connection of approximation in policy space with classification; cf. Fig. 4.1.2 and the discussion of Section 4.1. 
Classification is an important subject in machine learning. The objective is to construct an algorithm, called a classifier , which assigns a given “object” to one of a finite number of “categories” based on its “characteristics.” Here we use the term “object” generically. In some cases, the classification may relate to persons or situations. In other cases, an object may represent a hypothesis, and the problem is to decide which of the hypotheses is true, based on some data. In the context of approximation in policy space, objects correspond to states, and categories correspond to controls to be applied at the di!erent states . Thus in this case, we view each sample 
!

as an object-category pair. Generally, in (multiclass) classification we assume that we have a 
population of objects, each belonging to one of m categories c = 1, . . . ,m. We want to be able to assign a category to any object that is presented to us. Mathematically, we represent an object with a vector x (e.g., some raw description or a vector of features of the object), and we aim to construct a rule that assigns to every possible object x a unique category c. 
To illustrate a popular classification method, let us assume that if we draw an object x at random from this population, the conditional probability of the object being of category c is p(c |x). If we know the probabilities p(c |x), we can use a classical statistical approach, whereby we assign x to the category c!(x) that has maximal posterior probability, i.e., 
c!(x) ! arg max c=1,...,m 
p(c |x). (4.29) 
This is called the Maximum a Posteriori rule (or MAP rule for short; see for example the book [BeT08], Section 8.2, for a discussion). 
When the probabilities p(c |x) are unknown, we may try to estimate them using a least squares optimization, based on the following property, whose proof is outlined in Exercise 4.1; see also [Ber19a], Section 3.5.

In the context of DP and approximation in policy space, this classifier may be used, among others, in stopping problems where there are just two controls available at each state: stopping (i.e., moving to a termination state) and continuing (i.e., moving to some nontermination state). 
There are several variations of the preceding classification schemes, for which we refer to the specialized literature. Moreover, there are several commercially and publicly available software packages for solving the associated regression problems and their variants. They can be brought to bear on the problem of parametric approximation in policy space using any training set of state-control pairs, regardless of how it was obtained.

4.4.2 Perpetual Rollout with Value and Policy Networks -Multiprocessor Parallelization 
As we have noted in Section 2.1.3, it is possible to start with a base policy and a terminal cost approximation, and generate state-control samples of the corresponding truncated rollout policy. These samples can in turn be used with the approximation in policy space scheme of this section to obtain a policy network that approximates the truncated rollout policy; cf. Fig. 4.4.3. 
The cost function of the policy network can in turn be approximated with a value network using the methodology of Section 4.3. Then the value network can be used as a terminal cost function approximation in a truncated rollout scheme where the previously obtained policy network can be used as a base policy. In this way a perpetual rollout scheme is obtained, which involves a sequence of value and policy networks. 
Parallelization and distributed computation can be used in several di!erent ways in such a scheme, including Q-factor, Monte Carlo, and multiagent parallelization; see Section 2.4.5. Moreover, when feature-based partitioning of the state space is used (cf. Example 4.1.8), we may consider a multiprocessor parallelization scheme, which involves multiple local value and policy networks, one per subset of the state space partition; see Fig. 4.4.4. 
Let us finally note that multiprocessor parallelization leads to the idea of an approximation architecture that involves a graph. Each node of the graph consists of a neural network and each arc connecting a pair of nodes corresponds to data transfer between the corresponding neural networks.

Figure 4.4.4 Illustration of a perpetual truncated rollout scheme with a partitioned architecture. A local value network and a local policy network are used for each subset of the partition. The policy network is used as the base policy and the value network is used to provide a terminal cost function approximation. 
State-control training pairs for the corresponding rollout policy are obtained by starting at an initial state within some subset of the partition, generating rollout trajectories using the local policy network, which are truncated once the state enters a di!erent subset of the partition, with the corresponding terminal cost function approximation supplied by the value network of that subset. 
When a separate processor is used for each subset of partition, the corresponding value networks are communicated between processors. This can be done asynchronously, with each processor sharing its value network as soon it becomes available. In a variation of this scheme, the local policy networks may also be shared selectively among processors for selective use in the truncated rollout process. 
The question of how to train such an architecture is quite complex and one may think of several alternative possibilities. For example the training may be collaborative with the exchange of training results and/or training data communicated periodically or asynchronously. Ideas of asynchronous training of partitioned architectures are discussed in Section 5.8. 
4.5 NOTES AND SOURCES 
Section 4.1: Our discussion of approximation architectures, neural networks, and training has been limited, and aimed just to provide the connection with approximate DP. The literature on the subject is vast, and some of the textbooks mentioned in the references to Chapter 1 provide detailed
326 Learning Values and Policies Chap. 4 
accounts and many sources, in addition to the ones given in Sections 4.1 and 4.2. 
There are two broad directions of inquiry in parametric architectures: 
(1) The design of architectures, either in a general or a problem-specific context. 
(2) The training of neural networks, as well as other linear and nonlinear architectures. 
Research on both of these issues has been extensive and is continuing. An important direction, which we have emphasized here, is how to take advantage of distributed computation, particularly in conjunction with partitioned architectures (see also the neuro-dynamic programming textbook [BeT96], Section 3.1.3). 
Methods for selection of basis functions have received much attention, particularly in the context of neural network research and deep reinforcement learning (see e.g., the book by Goodfellow, Bengio, and Courville [GBC16]). For discussions that are focused outside the neural network area, see Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis [BeT96], Keller, Mannor, and Precup [KMP06], Jung and Polani [JuP07], Bertsekas and Yu [BeY09], and Bhat-nagar, Borkar, and Prashanth [BBP13]. Moreover, there has been considerable research on optimal feature selection within given parametric classes (see Menache, Mannor, and Shimkin [MMS05], Yu and Bertsekas [YuB09], Busoniu et al. [BBD10a], and Di Castro and Mannor [DiM10]). 
Incremental algorithms are the principal methods for training approximation architectures. They are supported by substantial theoretical analysis, which addresses issues of convergence, rate of convergence, stepsize selection, and component order selection. Moreover, incremental algorithms have been extended to constrained optimization settings, where the constraints are also treated incrementally, first by Nedić [Ned11], and then by several other authors: Bertsekas [Ber11a], Wang and Bertsekas [WaB15], [WaB16], Bianchi [Bia16], Iusem, Jofre, and Thompson [IJT18]. It is beyond our scope to cover this analysis. The author’s surveys [Ber10a] and [Ber15b], and convex optimization and nonlinear programming textbooks [Ber15a], [Ber16], collectively contain an extensive account of incremental methods, including the Kaczmarz, incremental gradient, subgradient, aggregated gradient, Newton, Gauss-Newton, and extended Kalman filtering methods, and give many references. The book [BeT96] and paper [BeT00] by Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis, and the survey by Bottou, Curtis, and Nocedal [BCN18] provide theoretically oriented treatments. 
Section 4.2: The publicly and commercially available neural network training programs incorporate heuristics for scaling and preprocessing data, stepsize selection, initialization, etc, which can be very e!ective in specialized problem domains. We refer to books on neural networks such as Bishop [Bis95], Goodfellow, Bengio, and Courville [GBC16], and Haykin [Hay08].
Sec. 4.5 Notes and Sources 327 
Deep neural networks have created a lot of excitement in the machine learning field, in view of some high profile successes in image and speech recognition, and in RL with the AlphaGo and AlphaZero programs. One question is whether and for what classes of target functions we can enhance approximation power by increasing the number of layers while keeping the number of weights constant. For analysis and speculation around this question, see Bengio [Ben09], Liang and Srikant [LiS16], Yarotsky [Yar17], Daubechies et al. [DDF19], and the references quoted there. 
Another important research question relates to the role of overparametrization in the success of deep neural networks. With more weights than training data, the training problem has infinitely many solutions. The question then is how to select a solution that works well on test data (i.e., data outside the training set); see Zhang et al. [ZBH16], [ZBH21], Belkin, Ma, and Mandal [BMM18], Belkin, Rakhlin, and Tsybakov [BRT18], Soltano-lkotabi, Javanmard, and Lee [SJL18], Bartlett et al. [BLL19], Hastie et al. [HMR19], Muthukumar, Vodrahalli, and Sahai [MVS19], Su and Yang [SuY19], Sun [Sun19], and the discussion in the book by Hardt and Recht [HaR21]. 
Section 4.3: Fitted value iteration has a long history; it was mentioned by Bellman among others. It has interesting properties, and at times exhibits pathological/unstable behavior due to accumulation of errors over a long horizon (see [Ber19a], Section 5.2). 
Advantage updating was proposed by Baird [Bai93], [Bai94], and is discussed further in Section 6.6 of the neuro-dynamic programming book [BeT96]. The di!erential training approach of Section 4.3.4 was proposed by the author in the paper [Ber97b], and followup work was presented by Weaver and Baxter [WeB99]. 
Section 4.4: Classification (sometimes called “pattern classification” or “pattern recognition”) is a major subject in machine learning, for which there are many approaches, an extensive literature, and an abundance of public domain and commercial software; see e.g. the textbooks by Bishop [Bis95], [Bis06], and Duda, Hart, and Stork [DHS12]. Approximation in policy space was formulated as a classification problem in the context of DP by Lagoudakis and Parr [LaP03], and was followed up by several other authors (see e.g., Dimitrakakis and Lagoudakis [DiL08], Lazaric, Ghavamzadeh, and Munos [LGM10], Gabillon et al. [GLG11], Liu and Wei [LiW14], Farahmand et al. [FPB15], and the references quoted there). While we have focused on a classification approach that makes use of least squares regression and a parametric architecture, other classification methods may also be used. For example the paper [LaP03] discusses the use of nearest neighbor schemes, support vector machines, as well as neural networks. 
The multiprocessor parallelization ideas, using state space partitioning with multiple policy and value networks have been applied to large-scale
328 Learning Values and Policies Chap. 4 
POMDP problems in the paper by Bhattacharya et al. [BBW20]. Asyn-chronous policy iteration with a partitioned architecture has been analyzed by Bertsekas and Yu [BeY10], [BeY12], [YuB13] for the case of lookup table representation of policies and cost functions. It will be discussed in greater detail in Chapter 5, in the context of infinite horizon problems.

Sec. 5.0 331 
In this chapter, we discuss rollout and approximate policy iteration (PI) methods for infinite horizon problems, including multiagent and distributed asynchronous versions. We have briefly discussed infinite horizon problems in Chapter 1, and we have described their structure (cf. Section 1.3.3). They di!er from their finite horizon counterparts in two main respects: 
(a) The number of stages is infinite. 
(b) The system is stationary, i.e., the system equation, 
xk+1 = f(xk, uk, wk), 
the cost per stage g(xk, uk, wk), and the probability distributions of the disturbance wk do not change with k. 
We aim to minimize the total cost over an infinite number of stages, given by 
J!(x0) = lim N!" 
E wk 
k=0,1,...

k=0

$ % 
. 
Here, J!(x0) denotes the cost associated with an initial state x0 and a policy " = {µ0, µ1, . . .}, and ! is a positive scalar, which may be strictly less that 1, in which case it has the meaning of a discount factor , or it may be equal to 1. At each state xk, there is a control constraint uk ! U(xk) and policies should satisfy this constraint, i.e., µk(xk) ! U(xk) for all stages k and states xk.† 
The optimal cost (the minimum over ") starting from x0 is denoted by J*(x0). If " is stationary, i.e., it has the form {µ, µ, . . .} for some function µ with µ(x) ! U(x) for all x, we also denote J! by Jµ. For the problems that we discuss in this chapter, the optimal value J*(x) is attained by a stationary policy, under our assumptions. This is also true for many (but not all) of the major types of infinite horizon DP problems. For this reason, we emphasize stationary policies in our development. 
Policies that attain the minimum cost simultaneously from all initial states are called optimal . We will aim to compute or characterize the optimal cost function J* as well as optimal stationary policies. As in the finite horizon discussions of Chapters 2-4, we will also consider a variety of approximation methods, and we will place primary emphasis on methods that rely on rollout and PI ideas. 
† Infinite horizon DP problems are often referred to as Markovian decision 
problems (MDP for short). We will use this name as well when there is stochastic structure that defines a (controlled) Markov chain. However, since our treatment 
of DP problems in this book is balanced between stochastic, deterministic, com-
binatorial, and minimax problems, we use the term “MDP” only on occasions where the problem has a clear Markov chain character.
332 Infinite Horizon Problems Chap. 5 
Our models and algorithms will progressively become more general, but we will initially focus on two types of problems, which we briefly described in Section 1.3.3. 
(a) Stochastic shortest path problems (SSP for short). Here, ! = 1 but there is a special cost-free termination state; once the system reaches that state it remains there at no further cost. We assume a finite number of states and controls at each state. This simplifies greatly the associated analytical and computational issues. The case of an infinite number of states is considerably more complex, but we will also note later that even with a finite number of states, significant complications arise if there are stationary policies under which the termination state may never be reached starting from some initial states. Policies of this kind are common, and will be called improper . By contrast, if all stationary policies are proper (i.e., the termination state is reached eventually, starting from any initial state, regardless of the policy used), the solution of the problem is significantly facilitated. 
(b) Discounted problems . Here, ! < 1, the number of states is finite, but there need not be a termination state. However, we will see that a discounted problem can be readily converted to a nicely-structured SSP problem, where all policies are proper. As a result, algorithms and analysis for SSP problems can often be easily applied to discounted problems. 
We provide the main analytical and algorithmic theory for these two problems in the next two sections. Except for a few new results, which are related to multiagent and distributed computational methods, the proofs may be found in several sources, including the RL book [Ber19a]. We will use the transition probability notation 
pxy(u) = P (xk+1 = y | xk = x, uk = u), 
for all possible values of (x, y, u). This notation is common and convenient for stochastic finite-state systems. 
It is important to note that the system equation and transition probability notational descriptions are equivalent. In particular, given the transition probabilities pxy(u), an equivalent system equation description is 
xk+1 = wk, 
where the disturbance wk is generated according to the distribution 
p(wk = y | xk = x, uk = u) = pxy(u). 
Conversely, given a system equation in the form xk+1 = f(xk, uk, wk) and the probability distribution of wk, the transition probabilities pxy(u) can
Sec. 5.1 Infinite Horizon Stochastic Problems 333 
be unambiguously calculated. By “equivalence” here we mean that if we start from the same initial state x0 and use the same policy, the probability distribution of the future states xk will be the same under the two system descriptions. Note that the transition probability notation has a simpler system equation, but a potentially more complicated probabilistic description (for example when the problem is deterministic, transition probabilities do not make sense). 
5.1 INFINITE HORIZON STOCHASTIC PROBLEMS 
5.1.1 Stochastic Shortest Path Problems 
We first consider the stochastic shortest path (SSP) problem, where we assume that there is no discounting (! = 1), and that there is a special cost-free termination state t. Once the system reaches that state, it remains there at no further cost, i.e., 
ptt(u) = 1, g(t, u, t) = 0, for all u ! U(t). 
In addition to the termination state, we assume that there are n states, which we denote by 1, . . . , n; see Fig. 5.1.1. 
We will provide rigorous statements of the analytical and algorithmic results, which we briefly mentioned in Sections 1.3.3 and 1.3.4, and we will transcribe them to our new notation. In particular, the Bellman equation and the value iteration algorithm (VI for short) take the following form.

Under our subsequent assumptions, the essence of the SSP problem is to reach the termination state t with minimum expected cost. In particular, while we allow policies that may never reach t, under our assumptions these policies cannot be optimal. To quantify this requirement we introduce a definition: we say that a stationary policy is proper if starting from any state and using that policy, the termination state t is guaranteed to be reached eventually. Equivalently the policy is proper if in the corresponding Markov chain every state is connected to t with a path of positive probability transitions. It can be seen that for a proper policy µ, the cost values Jµ(x), x = 1, . . . , n, are real numbers (since the expected number of stages to reach t from any state is finite, and the cost of each transition is bounded). A policy is called improper if it is not proper. 
Throughout this chapter, when discussing SSP problems, we will make the following assumption (or another assumption that implies it). 
Assumption 5.1.1: (SSP Conditions) The following hold for the SSP problem: 
(a) There exists at least one proper policy. 
(b) For every improper policy µ, there exists at least one state x such that Jµ(x) = ".
Sec. 5.1 Infinite Horizon Stochastic Problems 335 
An important special case is when the shortest path problem is deterministic. Then the preceding assumption translates to the conditions that every state is connected to t with at least one path, and that each cycle has positive length. These are the conditions under which the validity of deterministic shortest path algorithms is commonly proved. The subsequent four propositions generalize well known deterministic shortest path results, although their proofs are not elementary. They can be found in the original sources (Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis [BeT89], [BeT91]), or in textbooks such as [Ber12], [Ber18a]. 
Our first result is that the limiting form of the DP equation, Bellman’s equation, has the optimal cost function J* as its unique solution. This result and the next one that relates to the VI method depend critically on Assumption 5.1.1(b). The abstract DP monograph [Ber18a] considers at length the more complex case where this assumption does not hold, and as a result Bellman’s equation can have multiple solutions.

Our next result provides a necessary and su"cient condition for optimality of a proper policy. 
Proposition 5.1.4: (Optimality Condition) A proper policy µ is optimal if and only if for every state x, µ(x) attains the minimum in the Bellman equation (5.1). 
Note that an improper policy cannot be optimal under our Assump-tion 5.1.1. As a result, based on the above proposition, an improper policy cannot attain the minimum in the Bellman equation. Moreover, since the control space has been assumed to be finite, a policy attaining the minimum in Bellman’s equation must exist and it has to be proper. 
In the absence of the SSP conditions (Assumption 5.1.1), serious and uncommon complications may occur. In particular, Bellman’s equation may have no solution or an infinite number of solutions; see the subsequent Example 5.1.1. Moreover, it may have a unique solution, which is di!erent than J*; see the paper by Bertsekas and Yu [BeY16], and the abstract DP monograph [Ber18a], Section 3.1.2, which provide an example of this type that has an unusual structure but few states.

We refer to Eq. (5.3) as the variational form of Bellman’s equation, and to the modified cost per stage ĝ as the temporal di!erence corresponding to V . Temporal di!erences play a significant role in several algorithmic RL contexts; see the approximate DP/RL books noted earlier. 
Note that Eq. (5.3) is the Bellman equation for a cost-modified problem, where the cost per stage g has been replaced by the temporal di!erence ĝ. Thus by applying Prop. 5.1.1, we have that Ĵ = J* # V is the unique solution of this equation, so that J* can be obtained by solving either the original or the cost-modified version of the problem. Moreover, a policy µ has cost function Ĵµ = Jµ#V in the cost-modified problem. It follows that the original and the cost-modified SSP problems are essentially equivalent, and the choice of V does not matter when exact DP methods are used to solve them. However, when approximations are used, di!erent results may be obtained, which can be more favorable with an appropriate choice of V . 
In particular, we have the option to choose V and an approximation architecture methodology that matches the di!erential Ĵ = J* # V better than it matches J*. For example, we may obtain V with some problem approximation scheme as a rough estimate of J*, and then use a di!erent approximation in value space scheme, based on di!erent principles, for the corresponding cost-modified problem; see the discussion of state-dependent baselines in Section 4.3.3. We refer to this as cost shaping (the name “reward shaping” is used in the RL literature, for problems involving reward maximization). 
While cost shaping does not change the optimal policies of the original DP problem, it may change significantly the suboptimal policies produced by approximate DP methods, such as the ones we have discussed and will
338 Infinite Horizon Problems Chap. 5 
discuss further in this chapter. A key fact is that with a choice of V close to J*, the range of values of Ĵ is reduced, and this tends to enhance the ability of approximation methods to capture small scale variations in J*. This is similar to the motivation for approximating cost function di!erences (Sections 2.3.7, 2.4.4), and for advantage updating and di!erential training (Sections 4.3.3, 4.3.4).

Proposition 5.1.8: (Optimality Condition) A stationary policy µ is optimal if and only if for every state x, µ(x) attains the minimum in the Bellman equation (5.5). 
Bellman’s equation (5.5) has a familiar DP interpretation. At state x, the optimal cost J*(x) is the minimum over all controls of the sum of the expected current stage cost and the expected optimal cost of all future stages. The former cost is g(x, u, y). The latter cost is J*(y), but since this cost starts accumulating after one stage, it is discounted by multiplication with !. 
Finally, let us mention that the cost shaping idea discussed for SSP problems, extends readily to discounted problems. In particular, for any

Q-Learning 
We will now discuss some algorithms that involve Q-factors and stochastic sampling. These algorithms are generically referred to as Q-learning, and are related to the VI algorithm, as well as to the PI methods that we will discuss in the next section. We will focus on the discounted problem; the books [BeT96] and [Ber12], and the papers [Tsi94] and [YuB13b] contain the theory of Q-learning for SSP problems.

The original and most widely known Q-learning algorithm ([Wat89]) is a stochastic version of VI, whereby the expected value in Eq. (5.6) is suitably approximated by sampling and simulation. In particular, an infinitely long sequence of state-control pairs 
( (xk, uk)

ing to some probabilistic mechanism. For each pair (xk, uk), a state yk is generated according to the probabilities pxkyk(uk). Then the Q-factor of (xk, uk) is updated using a stepsize #k ! (0, 1], while all other Q-factors are left unchanged: 
Qk+1(x, u) = (1 # #k)Qk(x, u) + #k(FkQk)(x, u), for all (x, u), (5.7) 
where

(5.8) Note that (FkQk)(xk, uk) is a single sample approximation of the expected value defining (FQk)(xk, uk) in Eq. (5.6). 
To guarantee the convergence of the algorithm (5.7)-(5.8) to the optimal Q-factors, some conditions must be satisfied. Chief among these are that all state-control pairs (x, u) must be generated infinitely often within the infinitely long sequence 
( (xk, uk) 
) , and that the successor states yk 
must be independently sampled at each occurrence of a given state-control pair. Furthermore, the stepsize #k should satisfy the conditions 
#k > 0, for all k, "

which are typical of stochastic approximation methods (see e.g, the books [BeT96], [Ber12], Section 6.1.4), as for example when #k = c1/(k + c2), where c1 and c2 are some positive constants. In addition some other technical conditions should hold. A mathematically rigorous convergence proof was given in the paper [Tsi94], which embeds Q-learning within a broad class of asynchronous stochastic approximation algorithms. This proof (also reproduced in the book [BeT96]) combines the theory of stochastic approximation algorithms with the convergence theory of asynchronous DP and asynchronous iterative methods; cf. the papers [Ber82], [Ber83], and the book [BeT89]. 
In practice, the preceding Q-learning algorithm has some drawbacks, the most important of which is that the number of Q-factors/state-control pairs (x, u) may be excessive. To alleviate this di"culty, we may introduce a Q-factor approximation architecture. We will discuss this possibility later in this chapter.

5.2 EXACT AND APPROXIMATE POLICY ITERATION 
In the preceding section we provided the main analytical results for SSP and discounted problems. We also discussed the VI algorithm and its convergence. All these results hold in their most favorable forms for the finite-state cases that we considered. In this section we will again focus on the SSP and discounted problems of the preceding section, and develop the fundamental method of policy iteration (PI for short) and its variations. 
We will also consider approximations, including various forms of rollout, which can be viewed as a single iteration of PI (or one of its variations). In particular, the idea of using value and policy networks in a form of repeated rollout, which we discussed in Section 2.1.3, will be adapted to the infinite horizon setting. Figure 5.2.1 illustrates some of the variants of rollout with single-step lookahead that we will consider. 
5.2.1 Policy Iteration and Rollout 
The PI algorithm is the major alternative to VI. It starts with a stationary policy µ0, and generates iteratively a sequence of new policies µ1, µ2, . . . . The algorithm has solid convergence guarantees when implemented in its exact form, as we have discussed in Section 1.3.4 and we will discuss in greater detail shortly. 
We recall the rollout algorithm where we start with some policy and produce an improved policy though a process of cost function evaluation and one-step or multistep lookahead minimization. The PI algorithm is an extension of this idea and consists of multiple successive policy evaluations and policy improvements, i.e., a form of perpetual rollout , which we discussed in Sections 1.3.4 and 2.1.3.

The cost improvement property is also indirectly responsible for the properness of all policies generated by PI in the SSP case. Intuitively, the reason is that the initial policy is assumed proper, and improper policies have infinite cost from some initial states according to the SSP conditions of Assumption 5.1.1. 
In practice, a lot of cost improvement is often obtained from the first few policies generated by the PI algorithm, particularly the first one, even if the number of iterations to terminate is quite large. This is consistent with practical experience with the single iteration/rollout algorithm, and with the view of PI as a form of Newton’s method (cf. Section 1.3.4). 
Rollout with Multiple Policies - Parallel Rollout 
As in the case of finite horizon problems, the rollout policy is the result of a single policy improvement using a base policy. Thus, based on Eq. (5.14), the rollout policy has improved cost function over the base policy. This property also extends to a form of parallel rollout where multiple policies are used simultaneously in a one-step lookahead minimization, similar to

Finally, we note that there is a similar result to Prop. 5.2.2 for SSP problems, which, however, requires that all the policies µ1, . . . , µm are proper. In this case, the rollout policy µ̃ is also proper.

5.3 VARIANTS OF POLICY ITERATION AND Q-LEARNING 
In this section we will consider several variations of PI, which aim to improve its computational requirements and its performance. Most of these variations have Q-learning counterparts, but we will discuss primarily on
356 Infinite Horizon Problems Chap. 5 
PI with cost functions, since PI for Q-factors may also be viewed as PI with costs in a suitably reformulated problem, as we have just noted. We focus exclusively on discounted problems to avoid some of the tricky issues associated with improper policies in SSP problems. 
5.3.1 Optimistic Policy Iteration and Truncated Rollout 
The PI algorithm that we have discussed so far uses exact policy evaluation of the current policy µk and one-step lookahead policy improvement, i.e., it computes exactly Jµk , and it obtains the next policy µk+1 by a one-step lookahead minimization using Jµk as an approximation to J*. We will now describe a more flexible algorithm, called optimistic PI, whereby Jµk is approximated by any number of VIs corresponding to µk (cf. Prop. 5.1.7). 
Optimistic PI aspires (somewhat “optimistically”) to obtain a good successor policy using an inaccurate evaluation of the current policy. It starts with a pair (J0, µ0) and generates a sequence of pairs 
( (Jk, µk) 
) . 
The kth iteration starts with a pair (Jk, µk), and performs mk iterations of the VI algorithm that corresponds to µk, starting with Jk. It then obtains µk+1 and Jk+1 by a form of policy improvement.

Optimistic PI has solid convergence properties, although it may require an infinite number of iterations to converge to J*. In particular, for the discounted problem, it can be shown that the sequence {Jk} generated
Sec. 5.3 Variants of Policy Iteration and Q-Learning 357 
by the optimistic PI algorithm satisfies Jk ( J*, while the generated policies µk are optimal for all k su"ciently large (see e.g., [Ber12], [Ber19a]). 
An interesting observation is that in the extreme case where mk = 0, the method consists of just the policy improvement operation and is essentially equivalent to the VI algorithm. Thus optimistic PI is intermediate between PI and VI, and combines characteristics of both algorithms. 
Truncated Rollout as a Single Optimistic Policy Iteration 
From Eq. (5.22), it can be seen that the evaluation step of optimistic PI consists of an approximation of Jµk by using µk for mk stages, and then by adding a “terminal cost approximation” equal to the current cost estimate Jk (instead of using µk for an additional infinite number of stages). Simulation-based implementations of optimistic PI operate according to this interpretation: they use one-step lookahead minimization, but they evaluate the cost function Jµk approximately, by using mk-stage trajectories, while accounting for the cost of future stages by adding the terminal cost approximation Jk. This is in e!ect truncated rollout, which at state xk performs a one-step lookahead minimization with cost function approximation obtained by mk-stages rollout using µk as the base policy, followed by terminal cost function approximation Jk. 
An interesting question is the choice of the number of stages of the truncated rollout, i.e., of the number mk. This question has received much attention in the context of optimistic PI, and the general conclusion is that the number of VIs to evaluate the current policy should be neither too large, nor too small, and that the optimal number is problem-dependent, and should be determined by experimentation. 
If we view truncated rollout as a single optimistic PI, we may also infer that the optimal number of rollout steps mk should be problem-dependent, and that it should also be determined by experimentation. Moreover, in rollout for stochastic problems the policy evaluation after a few steps can become very inaccurate due to simulation noise, so any computational e!ort to increase the length of the simulation (make mk larger) may be unwieldy, as practical experience seems to suggest. In addition, in discounted problems, errors far into the future do not matter much due to discounting, and this also argues for a shorter length of truncated rollout. 
5.3.2 Multistep Policy Iteration 
Multistep PI simply replaces the one-step lookahead policy improvement operation of exact and optimistic PI with a multistep lookahead minimization. The motivation is that this may yield a better policy µk+1 than the one obtained with one-step lookahead. This also applies to multistep rollout, and makes even more sense when the evaluation of µk is approximate, since then the longer lookahead may compensate for errors in the policy
358 Infinite Horizon Problems Chap. 5 
evaluation. For an example where long lookahead is very advantageous, think of the on-line player of AlphaZero. Exercise 5.2 also provides an intuitive explanation of the benefits of multistep lookahead in the context of approximation in value space and truncated rollout. 
We first give the method in its exact nonoptimistic form. We later discuss how it may be combined with optimistic PI.

Exact PI with multistep lookahead has the same solid convergence properties as its one-step lookahead counterpart. It terminates with an optimal policy, and the generated sequence of policies is monotonically improving. The proof is very similar to the one we have described for the one-step lookahead case in Section 5.2.1. 
There is also a multistep version of optimistic PI: the policy improvement operation uses multistep instead of one-step lookahead. One may prove convergence of the exact form of this method similar to both the optimistic and the multistep PI algorithms. 
Similar to the one-step case, we may view multistep lookahead truncated rollout, as a simulation-based implementation of a single multistep optimistic PI. Note here that the multistep lookahead minimization may be approximated with an adaptive sampling-based lookahead scheme such as Monte Carlo tree search; cf. Section 2.4.2.

5.3.3 Multiagent Rollout and Policy Iteration 
In this section we will modify and generalize the multiagent rollout ideas that we discussed in Section 3.2, so that they apply to infinite horizon problems and the PI context. We will focus on discounted problems, but a qualitatively similar methodology can be used for SSP problems, assuming that the initial policy is proper. 
In particular, we consider a stationary infinite horizon !-discounted version of the finite horizon m-agent problem of Section 3.2, where m > 1, ! ! (0, 1) is the discount factor, and the control is u = (u1, . . . , um). The component u", % = 1, . . . ,m, is chosen by agent %, from within a given state-dependent constraint set U"(x), i.e., the control constraint set U(x) has the Cartesian product form U(x) = U1(x) ) · · · ) Um(x). At state x, a control u is applied, and the transition to a next state y is generated according to transition probabilities pxy(u). 
An equivalent version of the problem, involving an expanded state space is depicted in Fig. 5.3.1 for the case m = 3. The state space of the reformulated problem consists of

At each stage, the agents choose their controls sequentially in a fixed order: from state x agent 1 applies u1 ! U1(x) to go to state (x, u1), then agent 2 applies u2 ! U2(x) to go to state (x, u1, u2), and so on, until finally at state

Note that this reformulation involves the type of tradeo! between control space complexity and state space complexity that we discussed in Section 3.2. The reformulated problem involves m cost-to-go functions

each state x independently, i.e., the computations for state x do not depend on the computations for other states, thus allowing the use of parallel computation over the di!erent states. On the other hand, the computations corresponding to individual control components must be performed in sequence. It will also be clear from the subsequent analysis that, for convergence purposes, the ordering of the components is not important, and it may change from one policy improvement operation to the next. In fact there are versions of the algorithm, which simultaneously optimize over multiple component orders, and are amenable to parallelization as discussed in Section 3.2. 
Similar to the finite horizon case of Section 3.2, the salient feature of the multiagent policy improvement operation (5.24) is that it is far more economical than the standard policy improvement: it requires a sequence ofm minimizations, once over each of the control components u1, ..., um. In particular, for the minimization over the typical component u", the preceding components u1, . . . , u"#1 have been computed earlier by the minimization that yielded the policy components µ̃1, . . . , µ̃"#1, while the following controls u"+1, . . . , um are determined by the current policy components µ"+1, . . . , µm. Thus, if the number of controls within each component constraint set U"(x) is bounded by a number q, the multiagent operation (5.24) requires at most qmn Q-factor calculations. 
By contrast, since the number of elements in the constraint set U(x) is bounded by qm, the corresponding number of Q-factor calculations in the standard policy improvement is bounded by qmn. Thus in the multiagent policy improvement the number of Q-factors grows linearly with m, as compared to the standard policy improvement, where the number of Q-factor calculations grows exponentially with m. 
Multipass Multiagent Policy Improvement 
In trying to understand why multiagent rollout of the form (5.23) succeeds in improving the performance of the base policy, it is useful to think of the multiagent policy improvement operation as a simplification of the standard policy improvement operation. In this sense it is related to the simplified rollout algorithm of Section 2.3.3. We basically approximate the joint minimization over all the control components u1, . . . , um with a single “coordinate descent-type” iteration, i.e., a round of single control

Convergence to an Agent-by-Agent Optimal Policy 
An important fact is that multiagent PI need not converge to an optimal policy. Instead we will show convergence to a di!erent type of optimal policy, which we will now define. 
We say that a policy µ = {µ1, . . . , µm} is agent-by-agent optimal if 
µ ! 5Mµ(Jµ), or equivalently [cf. Eq. (5.24)], if for all x = 1, . . . , n, and % = 1, . . . ,m, we have

To interpret this definition, let a policy µ = {µ1, . . . , µm} be given, and consider for every % ! {1, . . . ,m} the single agent DP problem where for all i $= % the ith policy components are fixed at µi, while the %th policy component is subject to optimization. Then by viewing the preceding definition as the optimality condition for all the single agent problems, we can conclude that µ is agent-by-agent optimal if each component µ" is optimal for the %th single agent problem; in other words by using µ", each agent % acts optimally, assuming all other agents i $= % use the corresponding policy components µi. Agent-by-agent optimal policies may also be viewed as a special type of Nash equilibrium in a multiperson game, where all persons share the same cost function. 
Note that an (overall) optimal policy is agent-by-agent optimal, but the reverse is not true as the following example shows. 
Example 5.3.1 (Counterexample for Agent-by-Agent Optimality) 
Consider an infinite horizon problem, which involves two agents (m = 2) and a single state x. Thus the state does not change and the costs of di"erent stages are decoupled (the problem is essentially static). Each of the two agents chooses between the two controls 0 and 1: u1 # {0, 1} and u2 # {0, 1}. The
364 Infinite Horizon Problems Chap. 5 
cost per stage g is equal to 2 if u1 %= u2, is equal to 1 if u1 = u2 = 0, and is equal to 0 if u1 = u2 = 1. The unique optimal policy is to apply 
µ1(x) = 1, µ2(x) = 1. 
However, it can be seen that the suboptimal policy that applies 
µ1(x) = 0, µ2(x) = 0 
is agent-by-agent optimal. 
The preceding example is representative of an entire class of DP problems where an agent-by-agent optimal policy is not overall optimal. Any static (single step) multivariable optimization problem where there are nonoptimal solutions that cannot be improved upon by coordinate descent can be turned into an infinite horizon DP example where these nonoptimal solutions define agent-by-agent optimal policies that are not overall optimal. Conversely, one may search for problem classes where an agent-by-agent optimal policy is guaranteed to be optimal among the type of multivariable optimization problems where coordinate descent is guaranteed to converge to an optimal solution. For example positive definite quadratic problems or problems involving di!erentiable strictly convex functions (see [Ber16], Section 3.7). Generally, agent-by-agent optimality may be viewed as an acceptable form of optimality for many types of problems. 
Our main result is that the multiagent PI algorithm generates a sequence of policies that converges in a finite number of iterations to a policy that is agent-by-agent optimal. Moreover, we will show that even if the final policy produced by multiagent PI is not optimal, each generated policy is no worse than its predecessor. In the presence of approximations, which are necessary for large problems, it appears that the policies produced by multiagent PI are often of su"cient quality for practical purposes, and no worse than the ones produced by other (far more computationally intensive) approximate PI methods to be discussed in what follows in this chapter. 
For the proof of our convergence result, we will use a special rule for breaking ties in the policy improvement operation in favor of the current policy component. This rule is easy to enforce, and guarantees that the algorithm cannot cycle between policies. Without this tie-breaking rule, the following proof shows that while the generated policies may cycle, the corresponding cost function values converge to a cost function value of some agent-by-agent optimal policy. 
In the following proof and later all vector inequalities are meant to be componentwise, i.e., for any two vectors J and J &, we write 
J & J & if J(x) & J &(x) for all x.

and after a finite number of iterations, we have µk+1 = µk, in which case the policies µk+1 and µk are agent-by-agent optimal.

Example 5.3.2 (Multiagent PI for Leader-Follower Problems) 
Let us consider multiagent PI applied to two-stage leader-follower problems as described in Example 3.2.3. Here we have assumed a leader who knowing the initial state x0, makes a decision u0 # U0 according to a policy µ0, and a state transition 
x1 = f0(x0, u0, w0) 
occurs with cost g0(x0, u0, w0), where w0 is a random disturbance. Then the followers, knowing x1, choose decisions u! 
1 # U!, ! = 1, . . . , m, according to policies µ! 
1, ! = 1, . . . ,m, and a terminal state 
x2 = f1(x1, u 1 1, . . . , u

where w1 is a random disturbance, is generated with cost 
g1,1(x1, u 1 1, w1) + · · ·+ g1,m(x1, u 
m 1 , w1) + g2(x2). 
The problem is to select a leader policy µ0 and follower policies µ! 1, ! = 
1, . . . ,m, so as to minimize the total expected cost. This is a two-stage DP problem, which can be very hard to solve for 
large m. In Example 3.2.3, we discussed the multiagent rollout algorithm for this problem. Repeated application of multiagent rollout, yields a multiagent PI method. This method admits a very similar analysis to the one given in this section. In particular, the sequence of generated policies is monotonically improving, and yields a policy for the leader and agent-by-agent optimal policies for the followers. These policies form a Nash equilibrium for the leader-follower problem. 
An important variant of multiagent PI is an optimistic version, whereby policy evaluation is performed by using a finite number of multiagent variants of value iteration. We will discuss schemes of this type later, in the context of multiagent VI in Section 5.6. 
There are also several possible versions for approximate multiagent PI, including the use of value and policy neural networks. In particular, the multiagent policy improvement operation (5.24) may be performed at a sample set of states xs, s = 1, . . . , q, thus yielding a training set of staterollout control pairs 
# xs, µ̃(xs) 
$ , s = 1, . . . , q, which can be used to train 
a (policy) neural network to generate an approximation µ̂ to the policy µ̃. The policy µ̂ can be used in turn to train a (value) neural network that approximates its cost function value Jµ̂, and the approximate multiagent policy iteration cycle can be continued. Thus in this scheme, the di"culty with a large control space is overcome by multiagent policy improvement, while the di"culty with a large state space is overcome by training value and policy networks.

a!ects the performance of the corresponding autonomous multiagent rollout algorithm. The simplest possibility is to use as signaling policy the base policy; i.e., 6µ = µ. However, this choice does not guarantee policy improvement and can lead to poor performance, as we have illustrated in Section 3.2. Still, using the base policy as signaling policy can be an attractive possibility, which one may wish to try (perhaps in some modified form) on specific problems, in view of its simplicity and its parallelization potential.†

Sec. 5.3 Variants of Policy Iteration and Q-Learning 369 
On the other hand, if the signaling policy is taken to be the (nonau-
tonomous) multiagent rollout policy µ̃ ! 5Mµ(Jµ) [cf. Eq. (5.24)], i.e., 6µ = µ̃, the autonomous and nonautonomous multiagent rollout policies coincide. Thus nothing is gained from the use of this signaling policy. 
A related interesting possibility is to choose the signaling policy 6µ to approximate the multiagent rollout policy µ̃ ! 5Mµ(Jµ). In particular, we may obtain the policy 6µ = (6µ1, . . . , 6µm#1), by problem approximation, whereby 6µ is the rollout policy for a related but simpler problem, such as a “certainty equivalent” version of the original problem, whereby the stochastic system is replaced by a deterministic one. In this case, the Monte Carlo simulation needed to approximate the actions of µ̃ will be replaced by deterministic single agent shortest path computations, with great simplifications resulting. 
Another interesting approach is to obtain 6µ with o!-line training and approximation in policy space using a neural network, where the training set is generated by the multiagent rollout policy µ̃ ! 5Mµ(Jµ). Here are two possibilities along these lines: 
(a) We may use the approximate multiagent PI algorithm with policy network approximation (cf. Section 4.4), start with some initial policy µ0, and produce k new policies µ1, . . . , µk. Then the rollout scheme would use µk as signaling policy, and µk#1 as base policy. The final rollout policy thus obtained can be implemented on-line with the possibility of on-line replanning and the attendant robustness property. 
(b) We may generate a base policy µ by a policy gradient or random search method, and approximate the corresponding multiagent rollout policy µ̃ ! 5Mµ(Jµ) by o!-line neural network training. Then the rollout scheme would use the neural network policy thus obtained as signaling policy, and µ as base policy. Again, the final rollout policy thus obtained can be implemented on-line with the possibility of online replanning and the attendant robustness property. 
Note that if the neural network were to provide a perfect approximation of the rollout policy, the policy defined by Eq. (5.29) would be the same as the rollout policy, as noted earlier. Thus, intuitively, if the neural network provides a good approximation of the rollout policy (5.24), the policy defined by Eq. (5.29) will have better performance than both the base policy and the signaling policy. This was confirmed by the computational results of the paper [BKB20], within the context of a multi-robot repair application. 
The advantage of autonomous multiagent rollout with neural network approximations is that it yields approximate policy improvement (to the extent that the functions 6µi are good approximations to µ̃i), while allowing the speedup a!orded by autonomous agent operation, as well as on-line replanning when the problem data varies over time. The following example
370 Infinite Horizon Problems Chap. 5 
aims to illustrate these ideas. 
Example 5.3.3 (Autonomous Spiders and Flies) 
Let us return to the two-spiders-and-two-flies problem of Examples 3.2.1 and 3.2.4, and use it as a test of the sensitivity of autonomous multiagent rollout algorithm with respect to variations in the signaling policy. Formally, we view the problem as an infinite horizon MDP of the stochastic shortest path type. Recall that the base policy moves each spider selfishly towards the closest surviving fly with no coordination with the other spider, while both the standard and the multiagent rollout algorithms are optimal. 
We will now apply autonomous multiagent rollout with a signaling policy that is arbitrary . This also includes the case where the signaling policy is an error-corrupted version of the standard (nonautonomous) multiagent rollout policy; cf. the preceding discussion. The errors can be viewed as the result of the approximation introduced by a policy network that aims to represent the multiagent rollout policy (which is optimal as discussed in Example 3.2.1). Then it can be verified that the autonomous multiagent rollout policy with arbitrary signaling policy acts optimally as long as the spiders are initially separated on the line by at least one unit. What is happening here is that the Q-factors that are minimized in Eq. (5.29) involve a first stage cost (which is fixed at 1 and is independent of the signaling policy), and the cost of the base policy Jµ(y) starting from the next state y, which is not su!ciently a"ected by the signaling policy 6µ to change the outcome of the Q-factor minimizations (5.29). 
On the other hand, we saw in Example 3.2.4 that if we use as signaling policy the base policy, and the two spiders start at the same position, the spiders cannot coordinate their move choices, and they never separate. Thus the algorithm gets locked onto an oscillation where the spiders keep moving together back and forth, and (in contrast with the base policy) never capture the flies! 
The preceding example shows how a misguided choice of signaling policy (namely the base policy), may lead to very poor performance starting from some initial states, but also a very good performance starting from other initial states. Since detecting the “bad” initial states may be tricky for a complicated problem, it seems that one should be careful to support with analysis (to the extent possible), as well as substantial experimentation the choice of a signaling policy. 
The example also illustrates a situation where approximation errors in the calculation of the signaling policy matter little. This is the case where at the current state the agents are su"ciently decoupled so that there is a dominant Q-factor in the minimization (5.29) whose dominance is not affected much by the choice of the signaling policy. As noted earlier, one may exploit this type of structure by dividing the agents in “coupled” groups, and require coordination of the rollout control selections only within each group, while the computation within di!erent groups may proceed in par-
Sec. 5.3 Variants of Policy Iteration and Q-Learning 371 
allel with a signaling policy such as the base policy. Then the computation time/overhead for selecting rollout controls one-agent-at-a-time using online simulation will be proportional to the size of the largest group rather than proportional to the number of agents.† Note, however, that the “coupled” groups may depend on the current state, and that deciding which agents to include within each group may not be easy. 
Analysis that quantifies the sensitivity of the performance of the autonomous multiagent rollout policy with respect to problem structure is an interesting direction for further research. The importance of such an analysis is magnified by the significant implementation advantages of autonomous versus nonautonomous rollout schemes: the agents can compute on-line their respective controls asynchronously and in parallel without explicit inter-agent coordination, while taking advantage of local information for on-line replanning.

Types of Approximation in Value Space Schemes 
In Chapter 2 we described several types of multistep lookahead schemes, where J̃ is obtained in di!erent ways, such as problem approximation, rollout, and others. Some of these schemes can be fruitfully adapted to infinite horizon problems; see Figs. 5.2.1 and 5.3.2. For example, problem approximation approaches admit straightforward extensions to infinite horizon settings, whereby the function J̃(y) in Eq. (5.30) is obtained by solving exactly a DP problem that is related to the original in some way. 
The problem approximation approach is often interesting for partial state observation problems because a natural approximating problem is often evident. As we have noted in Section 1.4.4, such problems can be reformulated to ones involving perfect observation of the belief state, which, however, is infinite dimensional.† A particularly simple possibility is to derive the lookahead function J̃ by solving a perfect state information variant 
† Because of the infinite dimensionality of the belief space, the theory out-
lined earlier has to be extended before it can be applied to POMDP problems, 
since it was developed for finite state space. Usually this is fairly straightforward for discounted problems, but less so for SSP problems. We will not provide
Sec. 5.3 Variants of Policy Iteration and Q-Learning 373 
of the original problem, where an estimate of the system state is used as if it were exact. The perfect state information variant may be tractable, because it may be deterministic or it may involve a modest number of states. 
In this chapter, the approximation in value space schemes that we will focus on are primarily based on approximate (possibly optimistic) PI. They operate as follows, starting with an initial policy µ0: 
(a) We generate a sequence of policies µ0, µ1, . . .. 
(b) We evaluate (usually o!-line) each policy µk approximately, with a cost function J̃µk , often by using a parametric approximation/neural network approach. There is a large variety of policy evaluation algorithms; see the book [Ber12] and the survey paper [Ber11b].† 
(c) We generate the next policy µk+1 using one-step or multistep policy improvement based on J̃µk . This step, as well as step (b), may include the use of rollout truncation. 
We will view rollout as a simple form of approximate PI, which involves a single policy iteration, executed with the aid of simulation. The rollout may be truncated and supplemented with a terminal cost function approximation (which may be obtained with a sophisticated o!-line scheme). 
An important distinction is that rollout may be implemented online, possibly with the aid of simulation, or continuous control space optimization (as in MPC), whereas approximate PI ordinarily requires a value network and/or policy network approximation. In particular, since it is normally impossible to store for all states the values of a policy and its the exact cost function, it is inevitable that we have to approximate either the policy or its cost function or both by using some type of approximation architecture. This in turn necessitates the use of o!-line training.

In the case where the problem is undiscounted, i.e., ! = 1, there is typically a cost-free termination state, and a positive cost per stage for all non-termination states. In this case, the problem amounts to driving the state either exactly or asymptotically to the termination state at minimum cost. However, we do not need to assume the existence of a termination state. Note that our problem formulation includes classical control problems addressed by MPC, which involve a linear finite-dimensional system and a quadratic cost, as well as shortest path problems involving a graph with a finite number of nodes and nonnegative transition costs.

Unfortunately, our scheme (as stated above) is ill-defined because the problem defined by Eqs. (5.31)-(5.32) may not have a feasible solution. By this we mean that there may exist initial conditions x0 ! X for which the constraints (5.32) are violated for every feasible control sequence (uk, . . . , uk+"#1). To circumvent this di"culty, we may impose the following assumption, which is patterned after the constrained controllability condition for MPC (cf. Section 3.1.1). 
Invariance assumption: For every state x ! X , there exists a control u ! U(x) that keeps the next state within X , i.e., f(x, u) ! X . 
Since for a given problem, the state constraint set X may be such that the invariance assumption is violated, we follow a two-step solution approach:
