5.3.6 Implementation Issues of Parametric Policy Iteration 
Approximate PI in its various forms has been the subject of extensive research, both theoretical and applied. Let us provide a few comments, focusing on parametric PI schemes involving just a value network, i.e., a cost function approximation but not a policy approximation. 
Architectural Issues and Cost Shaping 
As can be expected, the choice of architectures for costs J̃µ(x, r) and Q-factors Q̃µ(x, u, r) is critical for the success of parametric approximation schemes for PI. These architectures may involve the use of features, and they could be linear, or they could be nonlinear such as a neural network. A major advantage of a linear feature-based architecture is that the corresponding policy evaluations involve linear least squares problems, which admit a closed-form solution. Moreover, when linear architectures are used, there is a broader variety of approximate policy evaluation methods with solid theoretical performance guarantees, such as TD(&), LSTD(&), and LSPE(&), which are described in detail in several RL textbooks. 
Another interesting possibility for architecture choice has to do with cost shaping, which we discussed in Section 5.1. This possibility involves a modified cost per stage 
ĝ(x, u, y) = g(x, u, y) + V (y)# V (x), x = 1, . . . , n, 
for SSP problems, where V can be any approximation to J* with V (t) = 0. The corresponding formula for discounted problems is 
ĝ(x, u, y) = g(x, u, y) + !V (y)# V (x), x = 1, . . . , n.
Sec. 5.3 Variants of Policy Iteration and Q-Learning 379 
As noted earlier, cost shaping may change significantly the suboptimal policies produced by approximate DP methods and approximate PI in particular. Generally, V should be chosen close (at least in terms of “shape”) to J* or to the current policy cost function Jµk , so that the di!erence J* # V or Jµk # V , respectively, can be approximated by an architecture that matches well the characteristics of the problem. It is possible to approximate V with a parametric architecture or some other approximation method, depending on the problem at hand. Moreover, in the context of approximate PI, the choice of V may change from one policy evaluation to the next. 
The papers referenced for Section 5.1 provide some applications of cost shaping (or reward shaping as it is sometimes called in RL contexts). An interesting possibility is to use complementary approximations for V and for J* or Jµk . For example V may be approximated with a neural network-based approach that aims to discover the general form of J* or Jµk , and then a di!erent method may be applied to provide a local correction to V in order to refine the approximation. 
Exploration Issues 
Generating an appropriate training set at the policy evaluation step of approximate PI poses considerable challenges, and the literature contains several related proposals. We will discuss the generic issue of inadequate exploration, which we noted earlier in connection with model-based approximate PI. This is indeed the Achilles’ heel of approximate simulation-based PI schemes, and is often not addressed seriously enough in practice. 
We recall that in parametric approximation of the cost function of a policy µ, we determine the value of the parameter vector r by generating a large number of training pairs (xs,'s), s = 1, . . . , q, where 's is a sample cost corresponding to xs and µ. We then use least squares training: 
r ! argmin r 
q" 
s=1 
# J̃µ(xs, r)# 's 
$2 . 
Each sample cost 's is generated by starting at xs, simulating a trajectory of states and controls using µ and the known transition probabilities for some number Ns of stages, accumulating the corresponding discounted costs, and adding a terminal cost approximation 
!Ns Ĵ(xNs), 
where xNs is the terminal state of the Ns-stage trajectory and Ĵ is some initial guess of Jµ. In this context, we may also employ trajectory reuse, which aims at reducing the sampling e!ort, by using the tail portions of any generated trajectory.
380 Infinite Horizon Problems Chap. 5 
Thus with trajectory reuse, we will be generating many cost or Q-factor samples that start from states frequently visited by µ, and this may bias the simulation by underrepresenting states that are unlikely to occur under µ. As a result, the cost estimates of these underrepresented states may be highly inaccurate, causing potentially serious errors in the calculation of the improved policy µ̃ via the policy improvement operation. 
One possibility to improve the exploration of the state space is to use a large number of initial states. It may then be necessary to use relatively short trajectories to keep the cost of the simulation low. To compensate for the short length of the trajectories it will then be important to introduce a terminal cost function approximation in the policy evaluation step in order to make the cost sample 's more accurate, as noted earlier. Moreover, when selecting the initial states of these trajectories, we should make sure that they are a representative sample of the portion of the state space most visited not just under the current policy, but also under other policies. 
A simple plausible scheme when evaluating policy µk, is to use randomization over a memory bu!er , which stores candidate initial states. In particular, we may use a set of initial states that consists of the union of multiple subsets X,X0, . . . , Xk#1, where X is a starting set of initial states, and X0, . . . , Xk#1 are generated while evaluating the previous policies µ0, . . . , µk#1. Each subset Xm should consist of states generated while evaluating policy µm. We evaluate µk, by using short trajectories whose starting states are chosen randomly from the subsets X,X0, . . . , Xk#1 with probabilities that may reflect a bias toward more recent policies (i.e., the probability of selecting an initial state from set Xm should increase with m). At the same time, while evaluating policy µk, we generate the subset of states Xk to use when training the next policy µk+1. The initial subset X is special and should be carefully chosen so that it includes not only a subset of representative states, but also successor states under a variety of control choices. The fine details of such a scheme are likely to be settled by trial and error. 
Thus in the preceding scheme, all state transitions and associated transition costs used to generate the costs 's of the training set are generated by using the current policy µk. However, the set of initial states of the trajectories used to produce the cost samples is quite diverse: it is obtained by randomization over the union of the starting set X and the set X0 , · · · ,Xk#1, which corresponds to states visited by the preceding policies. 
A potential weakness of a scheme of the preceding type is the need for a good terminal cost function approximation. Such an approximation may not be easily available, particularly for SSP problems involving substantial “late costs;” for example when most of the cost is incurred upon reaching the terminal state. Generally, SSP problems often require “deep exploration,” i.e., long trajectories that reach or get close to the destination. 
Exploration schemes like the one just described may also be used in
Sec. 5.3 Variants of Policy Iteration and Q-Learning 381 
the context of model-free variants of approximate PI for Q-factors. In fact the need for exploration in the space of state-control pairs is more acute. Again we may generate short trajectories that start with state-control pairs chosen randomly within a set of pairs that are representative of several policies. 
Let us also note the possibility to partition the state space, and select a rich enough representative set of initial states for each set of the partition. This allows a better control of exploration, and also ushers the possibility of using a distributed policy evaluation algorithm for each set of the partition; see our earlier discussion in Section 4.4.2, and the papers [BeY10], [BeY12], [YuB13a]. 
There have also been other related approaches to improve exploration, particularly in connection with the temporal di!erence methods. In some of these approaches, trajectories are generated through a randomized mix of two policies: the policy being evaluated, sometimes called the target policy, to distinguish from the other policy, called the behavior policy that introduces enhanced exploration; see the end-of-chapter references. In the RL literature (see e.g., the book [SuB18]), methods that use a behavior policy are called o!-policy methods, while methods that do not are called on-policy methods. A commonly suggested scheme is to use as an o!-policy one that is “(-greedy,” i.e., that attains the minimum in the policy improvement phase within some threshold ( > 0, which is experimentally chosen. Note, however, that selecting ( in such a scheme can be tricky (for example di!erent values of ( may be appropriate for di!erent parts of the state space). 
It is important to note, however, that using a behavior policy biases the cost samples towards that policy. Special modifications are needed, which blend harmoniously the target and behavior policy objectives. Such modifications were first introduced by Bertsekas and Yu [BeY09] (Section 3) to deal with the solution of general linear systems of equations (not just Bellman equations of policies in discounted and SSP problems); see also the book [Ber12], Sections 6.4.2 and 7.3.1. 
Generally, e"cient sampling, and the issue of balancing exploration with the choice of promising controls (the exploration-exploitation tradeo!) is a subject of continuing research. Many authors have suggested practical schemes that may work in given contexts, including on-line situations. For some recent work, see the paper by Russo and Van Roy [RuV16], and the monograph [RVK18]. The paper by Osband, Van Roy, Russo, and Wen [OVR19] develops special schemes to deal with issues of deep exploration. 
5.3.7 Optimistic Policy Iteration with Parametric Q-Factor Approximation - SARSA and DQN 
In Section 5.1.3, we discussed Q-learning algorithms with an exact representation of Q-factors. We will now consider Q-learning with Q-factor
382 Infinite Horizon Problems Chap. 5 
approximation. As we noted earlier (cf. Fig. 5.1.3), we may view Q-factors as optimal costs of a certain discounted DP problem, whose states are the state-control pairs (x, u) in addition to the original states. We may thus apply the approximate PI methods discussed earlier. For this, we need to introduce a parametric architecture Q̃(x, u, r). This architecture could be linear feature-based, or nonlinear such as one that uses a neural network. There are also optimistic approximate PI algorithms with Q-factor approximation, which involve truncated rollout. They use the current policy for a limited number of stages with cost function approximation for the remaining states, and/or a few samples in between policy updates. 
As an example, let us consider an extreme version that uses a single sample between policy updates. At the start of iteration k, we have the current parameter vector rk, we are at some state xk, and we have chosen a control uk. Then:

Sec. 5.4 Performance Bounds 383 
Extreme optimistic schemes of the type just described have been used in practice, and are often referred to as SARSA (State-Action-Reward-State-Action); see e.g., the books [BeT96], [BBD10], [SuB18]. When Q-factor approximation is used, their behavior is very complex, their theoretical convergence properties are unclear, and there are no associated performance bounds in the literature. The methods are more commonly used in a less extreme/optimistic form, whereby several (perhaps many) state-control-transition cost-next state samples are batched together and suitably averaged before updating the vector rk. 
Other variants of SARSA attempt to save in sampling e!ort by storing the generated samples in a bu!er and reusing them in some randomized fashion in subsequent iterations. This is also called sometimes experience replay, an idea that has been used since the early days of RL, both to save in sampling e!ort and to enhance exploration. The DQN (Deep Q Network) scheme, championed by DeepMind (see Mnih et al. [MKS15]), is based on this idea. Note, however, that experience replay does not depend on the use of a deep neural network architecture.

The bound (5.39) suggests that performance is improved when the length % of the lookahead is increased, and also when the lookahead cost approximation J̃ is closer to the optimal cost J* (when modified with an optimal constant shift '). Note that we are not guaranteeing that multistep lookahead will lead to better performance than one-step lookahead; this is not necessarily true (see, e.g., Example 2.2.1 in [Ber19a]). It is the performance bound that is improved with multistep lookahead.

Rollout, Parallel Rollout, and Multiagent Rollout 
Let us first consider rollout in its pure form, where J̃ in Eq. (5.30) is the cost function of some stationary base policy µ. Thus, the rollout policy is the result of a single policy iteration starting from µ. The policy evaluation that yields the costs Jµ(y) needed for policy improvement may be done in any suitable way. Monte Carlo simulation (averaging the costs of many trajectories starting from y) is one major possibility. Of course if the problem is deterministic, a single simulation trajectory starting from y is su"cient, in which case the rollout policy is much less computationally demanding. Note also that in discounted problems the simulated trajectories can be truncated after a number of transitions, which is su"ciently large to make the cost of the remaining transitions insignificant in view of the discount factor. 
An important fact is that in the pure form of rollout, the rollout policy improves over the base policy, consistent with the finite horizon case. This is stated in the following proposition [a special case of Prop. 5.4.1(b) as

noted earlier], and it is to be expected since rollout is just a single policy iteration, so the general policy improvement property of PI applies.

Some of the insights provided by the preceding proposition are: 
(1) Part (a) of the proposition implies that as the size of lookahead % increases, the bound on the performance of the rollout policy also improves. This is consistent with practical experience, which indicates that long lookahead can mitigate the e!ects of various errors in value space approximation schemes. Moreover, assuming that µ is close to optimal (so that Tm 
µ J̃ is close to J* as m ( "), the bound on the performance of the rollout policy µ̃ improves as m increases (the improvement is enhanced if J̃ is also close to Jµ).† 
(2) Part (c) suggests that if J̃ is close to Jµ, the performance of the rollout policy µ̃ is nearly improved relative to the performance of the base policy µ. This is consistent with the cost improvement property of rollout, cf. Prop. 5.4.2. Part (b) admits a similar interpretation. 
In summary, the guidelines for truncated rollout that are suggested by the error bounds of Prop. 5.4.3 are to choose %, the lookahead size as large as practical, choose J̃ as close to Jµ or J* as possible, and choose µ as close to optimal as possible. It is not clear to what extent increasing m, the length of rollout of µ, improves performance, despite the fact that the bound (5.45) improves as m increases. Indeed, looking at the bound (5.43), it can be seen that if J̃ is close to J*, but µ is not close to optimal, the bound can deteriorate with increasing values of m. Moreover there are examples that suggest that m should not be chosen to be very large (see [Ber17a], Exercise 6.16). A small value of m is also beneficial in another way: it limits the amount of computation needed for rollout, and reduces the variance of the cost estimates. In practice, for an infinite horizon problem, m is ordinarily chosen in some empirical fashion.

Sec. 5.5 Abstract View of Infinite Horizon Problems 395 
5.5 ABSTRACT VIEW OF INFINITE HORIZON PROBLEMS 
We will now introduce an abstract DP model, which aims at generality and unification, as well as notational simplification. The rationale is that our results for SSP and discounted problems owe their validity to a few structural properties of the Bellman operators T and Tµ of Eqs. (5.9) and (5.10) (for the SSP case), and Eqs. (5.11) and (5.12) (for the discounted case). The most critical properties in this regard are contraction, which is present for some of the models discussed in the preceding sections, as well as the monotonicity, which is present in almost all DP models of practical interest. 
We are thus motivated to use an analytical approach, whereby for a given DP problem, we may investigate whether there is an underlying contraction mapping and if so, address the analytical and algorithmic issues by using an extension of the theory developed for discounted, as well as SSP problems for the case where all policies are proper.† 
For the remainder of the present chapter, we will adopt this abstract point of view. In particular, we will consider a general class of mappings that are patterned after those appearing in stochastic DP, but are more general: for example they apply to minimax problems, game theoretic problems, undiscounted DP problems, and even to important problems beyond DP. We discuss the properties of these mappings, keeping in mind the main analytical and algorithmic issues we have discussed so far, and thus address interesting DP questions in substantially greater generality than heretofore.

Policy Iteration 
We will now discuss an abstract form of PI. The algorithm maintains and updates a policy µk, starting from some initial policy µ0. 
Policy Iteration Given the Current Policy µk: 
Policy evaluation: We compute Jµk as the unique solution of the equation 
Jµk = TµkJµk . 
Policy improvement: We obtain a policy µk+1 that satisfies 
Tµk+1Jµk = TJµk . 
We assume that the minimum of H(x, u, Jµk ) over u ! U(x) is attained for all x ! X , so that the improved policy µk+1 is defined (we use this assumption for all the PI algorithms of this chapter). The following proposition establishes a basic cost improvement property, as well as finite convergence for the case where the set of policies is finite. For the proof, see Prop. 2.4.1 of [Ber18a]. 
Proposition 5.5.3: (Convergence of PI) Let {µk} be a sequence generated by the PI algorithm. Then for all k, we have Jµk+1 & Jµk , with equality if and only if µk is optimal. Moreover, we have 
lim k!"

and if the set of policies M is finite, µk is optimal for all su"ciently large k. 
In the case where the set of policies is infinite, we may assert the convergence of the sequence of generated policies under some compactness and continuity conditions, which we will not go into (see [Ber18a]).

Optimistic Policy Iteration and &-Policy Iteration 
We will now discuss optimistic variants of PI, where the policy evaluation 
Jµk = TµkJµk 
is approximated by using multiple value iterations. In the most straightforward of these methods, starting with a function J0 ! B(X), we generate sequences {Jk} and {µk} with the algorithm 
TµkJk = TJk, Jk+1 = Tmk µk Jk, k = 0, 1, . . . , (5.59) 
where {mk} is a sequence of positive integers. There is no systematic guideline for selecting the integers mk. Usually their best values are chosen empirically, and tend to be considerably larger than 1 (in the case where mk 1 1 the optimistic PI method coincides with the VI method). It is also possible to randomize the choice of mk, an idea that we will discuss shortly. 
Variants of optimistic PI include multistep versions and methods with approximations in the policy evaluation and policy improvement phases. A method that is conceptually similar to the optimistic PI method is the &-policy iteration method (&-PI for short), which is defined by 
TµkJk = TJk, Jk+1 = T ($)

To compare optimistic PI and &-PI, note that they both involve multiple applications of the VI mapping Tµk : a fixed number mk in the former case, and a geometrically weighted number in the latter case. In fact, we may 
view the &-PI iterate T ($) 
µk Jk as the expected value of the optimistic PI 
iterate Tmk µk Jµk when mk is chosen by a geometric probability distribution 
with parameter &. One of the reasons that make &-PI interesting is its relation with im-
portant RL methods, such as TD(&) and other temporal di!erence methods, on one hand, and the proximal algorithm of convex optimization on the other. In particular, in &-PI a policy evaluation is performed with a single iteration of an extrapolated proximal algorithm; see the paper [Ber18d]. Thus &-PI provides a bridge between RL (in the form of temporal di!erence methods) and convex algorithmic optimization (in the form of the

Randomized Optimistic Policy Iteration Assuming a Finite Number of Policies 
We will now consider a randomized version of the optimistic PI algorithm, assuming that the set of policies M is finite. Its convergence can be proved much more simply than for nonrandomized optimistic PI (cf. Prop. 5.5.4). Significantly for our purposes, the convergence proof embodies ideas that will be used to formulate a convergent distributed asynchronous optimistic PI algorithm in Section 5.8.1.

5.6 MULTIAGENT VALUE AND POLICY ITERATION 
We will now consider a multiagent version of the abstract DP problem of the preceding section. It is patterned after the discounted multiagent PI algorithm of Section 5.3.3. The distinguishing feature of the problem is that the control u consists of m components u", % = 1, . . . ,m, where m > 1: 
u = (u1, . . . , um). (5.63) 
As earlier, each component may be viewed as being chosen by a distinct agent, with knowledge of the earlier selections of the other agents. We consider VI and PI algorithms that involve minimization component-by-component as opposed to minimization over all components at once. 
Similar to the finite horizon case and discounted cases of Sections 3.2 and 5.3.3, component-by-component minimization can lead to dramatic gains in computational e"ciency for large and even moderate values of m. In addition to a PI method, we discuss VI and optimistic PI methods, and we show their convergence to an agent-by-agent optimal policy, a type of policy that we considered for discounted problems in Section 5.3.3. 
We will develop our multiagent VI algorithm within the abstract framework of Section 5.5. We recall the key structure of this framework, which is the mapping H : X ) U ) R(X) .( /, where / denotes the real line and R(X) denotes the set of real-valued functions J : X .( /. The

For the multiagent structure, we assume that the control u consists of the m components u", % = 1, . . . ,m, [cf. Eq. (5.63)]. Moreover, we assume a finite set X of states and a finite set U of controls .† As a result, the control constraint set U(x) and the set of policies M are also finite, so the minimum of various expressions over U(x) or M is attained. Moreover, the space B(X) coincides with the space R(X) (the space of functions J on X with real-valued components). 
Note that in Section 5.3.3, we made a stronger assumption: we assumed that each control component u", % = 1, . . . ,m, is separately constrained to lie in a given finite set U"(x). Then U(x) is the Cartesian product set

In this section, we do not impose this assumption, except occasionally to discuss its implications. As a result our algorithms must ensure that the selection of a control component at a given state and stage does not preclude the feasibility of selection of the other control components at the same state and stage.

5.6.1 Convergence to an Agent-by-Agent Optimal Policy 
We will prove that the multiagent VI algorithm (5.70) converges to an agent-by-agent optimal policy, which we define as follows.

(Jµ, µ) ! 9P(Jµ, µ),

To interpret this definition, let a policy µ = {µ1, . . . , µm} be given, and consider, for every % = 1, . . . ,m, the single agent DP problem where for all %& $= % the %&th policy components are fixed at µ"# , while the %th policy component is subject to optimization. The definition (5.71) is the optimality condition for all these single agent problems [Eq. (5.71) can be written as Tµ,"Jµ = T"Jµ, where T" and Tµ," are the Bellman operators that correspond to the single agent problem involving agent %]. We can then conclude that µ = {µ1, . . . , µm} is agent-by-agent optimal if each component µ" is optimal for the %th single agent problem, where it is assumed that the other policy components remain fixed; in other words by using µ", each agent % acts optimally, assuming all other agents %& $= % continue to use the corresponding policy components µ"# . 
Note that an (overall) optimal policy is agent-by-agent optimal, but the reverse may not be true, as shown in Example 5.3.1. This is similar to what may happen in coordinate descent methods for multivariable optimization, where it is possible (in the absence of favorable assumptions) to stop at a nonoptimal point where no progress can be made along any one coordinate. As noted in Section 5.3.3, the notion of agent-by-agent optimality is related to the notion of person-by-person optimal solutions in team theory (see the end-of-chapter references), and may also be viewed as a special type of Nash equilibrium in a multiperson game, where all persons share the same cost function. 
While an agent-by-agent optimal policy may be either optimal or adequate for practical purposes, it may o!er no guarantees of quality. For a simple example, let U(x) be the intersection of a Cartesian product of finite subsets U"(x) of the real line and the unit simplex: 
U(x) = ( U1(x) ) · · ·) Um(x) 
) + {u | u1 + · · ·+ um = 1}.

Then it can be seen that the constraint set U",µ(x) consists of just the single point µ"(x), so that all feasible policies are agent-by-agent optimal. This is due to the extreme coupling of the control components through the simplex constraint. It would not happen if the constraint set was just a Cartesian product U1(x)) · · ·) Um(x), in which case we would have 
U",µ(x) = U"(x) 
for all %. Nonetheless, one should be aware that the method of partitioning of the control into components may seriously impact the e!ectiveness of our multiagent VI algorithm through the creation of spurious agent-by-agent optimal policies. 
We will now prove our main convergence result, under the following assumption, which is reminiscent of strict convexity assumptions in the analysis of coordinate descent methods (see e.g., [Ber16], Section 3.7). While we do not have a concrete counterexample, we speculate, based on experience with coordinate descent methods, that the assumption cannot be easily dispensed with.

Note that the preceding proposition does not guarantee convergence to the optimal policy (which is unique by Assumption 5.6.1). In particular, if our algorithm is started at a pair (Jµ̄, µ̄), where µ̄ is an agent-by-agent optimal policy, it will not move from µ̄ [in fact it can be shown that this will happen even if the algorithm is started at a pair (J0, µ̄), where J0 is su"ciently close to Jµ̄]. Thus every agent-by-agent optimal policy behaves roughly like a “local minimum,” with its own “region of attraction,” and is a potential convergence limit of our algorithm. The limit will depend on the starting pair, as well as the order in which the agents select their components. The algorithm guarantees convergence to the optimal policy only under additional assumptions that guarantee that there are no additional agent-by-agent optimal policies. 
Another possibility to enhance the convergence properties of the algorithm, and ensure convergence to an optimal policy, is to enlarge the constraint sets 
U",(µ̂1,...,µ̂!%1,µ!,...,µm)(x) 
in Eq. (5.67), to allow minimization over subsets of multiple control components. These subsets may be selected with some form of randomization: at some iterations minimize over a single control component as in iteration (5.67)-(5.68), while at some other randomly chosen iterations minimize over multiple or even all control components. Randomization over sets of multiple control components can also be used in the context of the optimistic
414 Infinite Horizon Problems Chap. 5 
agent-by-agent PI methods of the next section, and they can similarly enhance their convergence properties. We will not consider randomized control component selection schemes within the multiagent context further. Their principal drawback is that simultaneous minimization over multiple control components can be very costly (depending on the number of components involved), even if it is used in only a small proportion of the total number of iterations. 
We finally note that the preceding discussion applies to exact forms of multiagent VI. When approximations of various types are introduced, it may be hard to make predictions about the performance of the algorithm. 
5.6.2 Optimistic Multiagent Policy Iteration Algorithms 
In the preceding algorithm (5.70), each iteration involves a policy improvement operation, i.e., an m-step minimization that cycles through all control components one-by-one. We may also consider an optimistic PI variant where the m-step minimization is performed for only an infinite subset K * {0, 1, . . .} of the iterations, while for the complementary subset of iterations, k /! We call the algorithm (5.79)-(5.80)multiagent optimistic PI . It is a natural multiagent extension of the standard (single agent) optimistic PI algorithm (cf. Section 5.3.1). Note that when K = {0, 1, . . .}, the optimistic PI algorithm is the same as the multiagent VI algorithm (5.70). In cases where K is a “small” subset of {0, 1, . . .}, the multiagent optimistic PI algorithm involves nearly exact policy evaluations and “approaches” the multiagent PI algorithm of Section 5.3.3. 
Let us now consider the convergence of the optimistic PI algorithm (5.79)-(5.80). We have the following result. 
Proposition 5.6.2: (Optimistic PI Convergence to an Agent-by-Agent Optimal Policy) Let the assumptions of Prop. 5.6.1 hold, and let {Jk, µk} be a sequence generated by the optimistic agent-by-agent PI algorithm (5.79)-(5.80). Then there is an index k such that for all k ' k, we will have µk = µ̄, where µ̄ is an agent-by-agent optimal policy, while the sequence {Jk} will converge to Jµ̄.

Conditions for Obtaining an Optimal Policy 
We proved earlier that our multiagent VI algorithm will find an agent-by-agent optimal policy under our assumptions of Prop. 5.6.1, but this policy need not be optimal overall. We will now speculate on approaches that can be used to show that the policy obtained is optimal, under the same or alternative assumptions. One possibility is to impose conditions under which every agent-by-agent optimal policy is optimal. To this end we introduce the following definition.

Proposition 5.6.3: (Agent-by-Agent Optimality Criterion) As-sume that for every state x ! X and policy µ̄ such that µ̄(x) is a component-by-component minimum of H at (x, Jµ̄), the control µ̄(x) minimizes H(x, u, Jµ̄) over u ! U(x). Then every agent-by-agent optimal policy is optimal.

Proof: Let µ̄ be agent-by-agent optimal. Then from the definition of agent-by-agent optimality, we have that for all x ! X , µ̄(x) is a component-by-component minimum of H at (x, Jµ̄). By our assumption, this implies that for all x ! X , µ̄(x) minimizes H(x, u, Jµ̄) over u ! U(x), or Tµ̄Jµ̄ = TJµ̄. From general properties of contractive abstract DP models [cf. Prop. 5.5.1(a)], we also have Tµ̄Jµ̄ = Jµ̄. Hence Tµ̄Jµ̄ = TJµ̄, which implies that Jµ̄ = J* [cf. Prop. 5.5.1(e)], so µ̄ is optimal. Q.E.D. 
In view of Prop. 5.6.3, an important issue is to delineate su"cient conditions that guarantee that component-by-component minima of H at (x, Jµ) minimize H(x, u, Jµ) over u ! U(x). Somewhat similar questions have been addressed in two related contexts: 
(a) Team theory in connection with the notion of person-by-person optimality mentioned earlier. 
(b) The theory of convergence of coordinate descent methods in nonlinear optimization. 
In the theory of teams and other related decentralized control problem formulations, the most prominent analytical issues arise when the team members select control components based on di!erent information. By contrast in our framework the agents choose actions based on shared information, namely the current state xk of the system. Because of this fundamental structural assumption, DP algorithms such as VI and PI apply to our problem, but do not apply to team problems with nonclassical information pattens, exemplified by a famous counterexample of Witsen-hausen [Wit68]. 
In the theory of coordinate descent methods, the result most related to our context is that if a function F (y1, . . . , ym) of m vectors y1, . . . , ym is strictly convex and di!erentiable over the Cartesian product Y1 ) · · ·) Ym 
of closed convex sets Y1, . . . , Ym, then a vector ȳ = (ȳ1, . . . , ȳm) is a global minimum of F over Y1 ) · · ·) Ym if and only if it has the component-by-component minimization property 
ȳ" ! arg min y!$Y! 
F (ȳ1, . . . , ȳ"#1, y", ȳ"+1, . . . , ȳm), for all % = 1, . . . ,m. 
(5.81) Thus when F is strictly convex and di!erentiable, the block coordinate descent method cannot get trapped into a solution that is component-by-component minimum but is not a global minimum [this is not true, however, if F is strictly convex but nondi!erentiable, since the condition (5.81) may hold at vectors ȳ that are not global minima, and at which F is nondi!erentiable]. Some related results are known for the case where the sets Y" are discrete, under assumptions that can be loosely viewed as discrete space substitutes for strict convexity; see e.g., the papers [WaS00] and [BaP12].

Unfortunately, while the team theory and the coordinate descent results provide some analytical guidance, they do not apply directly to the DP context of this chapter. The reason is that the mapping H involves the functions Jµ, whose properties have to be verified through analysis. We leave this line of investigation as a subject for further research, and we outline another speculative analytical approach, which assumes continuous state and control spaces X and U , and is based on strict convexity and di!erentiability assumptions. 
Multiagent Algorithms for Continuous Spaces 
Let us consider removing the assumption that the state and control spaces X and U are finite, while continuing to assume that the control has m components, u = (u1, . . . , um) that are constrained by u ! U(x) for all x ! X . We continue to adopt the monotonicity and contraction Assumptions 5.5.1 and 5.5.2. Moreover, we assume that the various minima over control components in the definition of the algorithms are attained. Single-agent models of this type have been analyzed extensively in the abstract DP monograph [Ber18a] (Chapter 2), to which we refer for a detailed discussion. 
The definitions of agent-by-agent optimality and component-by-com-ponent minimum carry over without change to the continuous spaces setting, and so does the associated agent-by-agent optimality criterion (cf. Prop. 5.6.3). Furthermore, the key inequality (5.74) for the proof of the convergence result of Prop. 5.6.1 goes through, under the condition Tµ0J0 & J0 
[cf. Eq. (5.72)]. As a result, the proof of monotonic decrease of the sequence {Jk} to some function J̄ goes through as well. 
In conclusion, without assuming finiteness of the state and control spaces X and U , our algorithm, under the condition Tµ0J0 & J0 [cf. Eq. (5.72)], converges monotonically to some J̄ , which can be seen to be pointwise bounded below by the optimal cost function J*, so that J̄ ! B(X). Further conditions, involving strict convexity and di!erentiability, need to be imposed to guarantee that J̄ = J*, that J* is convex and di!erentiable, and that an optimal policy can be obtained. A stochastic optimal control model, involving a linear system, a convex cost per stage, and convex state and control constraints, was formulated and analyzed by the author in the paper [Ber73], and is well suited for this purpose. We leave further analysis along this line as a subject for further research.

Asynchronous Multiprocessor Parallelization 
The asynchronous PI algorithm (5.83)-(5.85) can be naturally implemented with value and policy approximations, and rollout truncation, as illustrated in Fig. 5.8.1. A value network or other approximation architecture may be used to approximate the cost functions of the generated policies. A policy network may also be used to approximate and implement the policies. Var-ious degrees of optimism can be introduced within the approximate policy
424 Infinite Horizon Problems Chap. 5 
evaluation using truncation of the simulation process, which generates the training data for the value networks. 
Moreover, when a separate processor is used for each subset of the partition, the corresponding value and policy network parameters are communicated between processors. This can be done asynchronously, with each processor sharing its value network parameters as soon as they become available. In a variation of this scheme, the local policy network parameters may also be shared selectively among processors for use in the truncated rollout process. These implementations are similar to the ones of Section 4.4.2 for finite horizon problems. 
Unfortunately, the theory supporting such distributed approximate PI schemes is weak, because several important aspects of the implementations are largely beyond the reach of analysis. These include the critical issue of exploration, which relates to the following dilemma: to evaluate e"ciently a policy µ, we often need to generate by simulation a lot of cost samples from states that are often visited under µ, but this may bias the simulation by underrepresenting states that are unlikely to occur under µ. As a result, the cost-to-go estimates of these underrepresented states may be highly inaccurate, causing potentially serious errors in the calculation of the “improved” policy via policy improvement. Other important implementation issues involve the choice and training of approximation architectures and the possibility that the sequence of policies obtained oscillates generically (not on an exceptional basis); see [Ber19a], Section 5.3.4. Thus the implementation of distributed approximate PI methods is a challenging art in practice. The reader may consult [BBW20] for a case study with a large-scale POMDP problem. 
Theoretical Convergence Issues 
It turns out, however, that even without the use of value and policy network approximations, the asynchronous PI algorithm (5.83)-(5.85) is still theoretically unreliable. The di"culty is that the algorithm involves a mix of applications of T and various mappings Tµ that have di!erent fixed points, so in the absence of some systematic tendency towards J* there is the possibility of oscillation (see Fig. 5.8.2). While this does not happen in synchronous versions, asynchronous versions of the algorithm may oscillate unless J0 satisfies some special sequential improvement-like condition, such as 
TJ0 & J0 
(examples of this type of oscillation have been constructed in the paper [WiB93]; see also [Ber10b], which translates an example from [WiB93] to the notation of the present book).

The proof of Prop. 5.8.1 shows that eventually, with probability one, after some iteration the algorithm will become equivalent to asynchronous VI (each policy evaluation will produce the same results as a policy improvement), while generating optimal policies exclusively. However, the expected number of iterations for this to happen can be very large. More-over the proof depends on the set of policies being finite. These observations raise questions regarding the practical e!ectiveness of the algorithm. However, it appears that for the great majority of practical problems the algorithm works well, and without unexpectedly slow convergence. The likely reason is that oscillatory behavior of (unmodified) asynchronous optimistic PI, of the type illustrated in Fig. 5.8.2, is apparently rare in practice, and seems to arise only in artificially constructed examples. 
A potentially important issue is the choice of the randomization probability p. If p is too small, convergence may be slow because oscillatory behavior may go unchecked for a long time. On the other hand if p is large, a correspondingly large number of policy improvement iterations may be performed, and the hoped for benefits of optimistic PI may be lost. Adaptive schemes which adjust p based on algorithmic progress may be an interesting possibility for addressing this issue.

Distributed Asynchronous PI Algorithm 
We now describe a PI algorithm, which applies asynchronously the components MFµ(V,Q) and Fµ(V,Q) of the mapping Gµ(V,Q) of Eq. (5.91). The first component is used for local policy improvement and makes a local update to V and µ, while the second component is used for local policy evaluation and makes a local update to Q. The algorithm draws its validity from the weighted maximum norm contraction property of Prop. 5.8.2(b) and the asynchronous convergence theory (Prop. 5.7.2). 
The algorithm is a modification of the “natural” asynchronous PI algorithm (5.84)-(5.85) [without the “communication delays” t# +"j(t)]. It generates sequences {V t, Qt, µt}, which will be shown to converge, in the sense that V t ( J*, Qt ( Q*. Note that this is not the only distributed iterative algorithm that can be constructed using the contraction property of Prop. 5.8.2, because this proposition allows a lot of freedom of choice for the policy µ. The paper by Bertsekas and Yu [BeY12] provides an extensive discussion of alternative possibilities, including stochastic simulation-based iterative algorithms, and algorithms that involve function approximation.

5.9 NOTES AND SOURCES 
Section 5.1: We have restricted ourselves to infinite horizon finite-state discounted and SSP problems with perfect state information. These problems and their semi-Markov versions are discussed in several textbooks; see e.g., [Ros70], [Put94], [Ber12], [Ber17a], and the RL book [Ber19a]. Several of these books also address the average cost problem, which we have not covered in this book. A discussion of the RL methodology for average cost problems can be found in the neuro-dynamic programming book [BeT96] (Section 7.1) as well as in the DP textbook [Ber12] (Section 7.2).
436 Infinite Horizon Problems Chap. 5 
Generally, infinite-state DP problems exhibit much more complex behaviors than finite-state MDP, and present many largely unresolved challenges for approximate DP methods. The theory of these problems is developed in a few books, including the author’s [Ber12] and [Ber18a]. The latter book, adopts the abstract formalism of Sections 5.5-5.8, and contains much recent research. It focuses on a broad variety of DP problems, including deterministic and stochastic infinite-state SSP, and highlights pathological behavior that may hamper the application of RL methods. 
An advanced treatment, which also addresses the complex probabilistic questions introduced by infinite disturbance spaces is given by Bertsekas and Shreve [BeS78]; see also the paper by Yu and Bertsekas [YuB15] for more recent supplementary work, which addresses the di"cult measurability questions that relate to PI in the context of infinite probability spaces. A treatment of the infinite spaces average cost problem that also includes the associated measurability questions has been given by H. Yu in [Yu20] and [Yu21]. 
The variational form of Bellman’s equation [cf. Eqs. (5.2)-(5.4)] has been used in various contexts, involving error bounds for VI, since the early days of DP theory, see e.g., [Ber12], Section 2.1.1. Within RL, the variational equation has been used in algorithmic settings under the name reward shaping or potential-based shaping (we have used the term “cost shaping” here as we are focusing on cost minimization); see the papers by Ng, Harada, and Russell [NHR99], Wiewiora [Wie03], Asmuth, Littman, and Zinkov [ALZ08], Devlin and Kudenko [DeK11], Grzes [Grz17] for some representative works. While reward shaping does not change the optimal policies of the original DP problem, it may change significantly the suboptimal policies produced by approximation in value space methods. Basically, with reward shaping and a linear feature-based approximation architecture, V is used as an extra feature. This is closely related to the idea of using approximate cost functions of policies as basis functions in approximation architectures, as suggested in the book [BeT96], Section 3.1.4. 
Section 5.2: The methods of VI and PI are the cornerstones of infinite horizon computational DP, and they serve as the principal points of departure for approximation in value space. Both of these methods were introduced by Bellman in his 1957 book [Bel57], and in earlier reports on which the book was based. Bellman’s analysis just introduced the basic methods, and proved their properties and their convergence in a limited number of special contexts. The methods and their variations have been discussed, generalized, and analyzed extensively in subsequent works. 
Sections 5.3.1-5.3.2: The idea of optimistic PI seems to have occurred simultaneously to several authors. It was first published and formally analyzed by van Nunen [Van76]. The papers by Puterman and Shin [PuS78], [PuS82] have also been influential. The connection of optimistic PI with truncated rollout has been emphasized in the author’s RL book [Ber19a].
Sec. 5.9 Notes and Sources 437 
An alternative to optimistic PI is &-PI, which was first proposed for discounted and SSP problems by Bertsekas and Io!e [BeI96]. The abstract form of this method was described in Section 5.5, and involves the operator 
T ($) µ , defined for a given & ! (0, 1) by

TµkJk = TJk, Jk+1 = T ($)

The books [BeT96], [Ber12], [Ber18a], the author’s review paper [Ber13b], and the references quoted there discuss exact and approximate forms of &-PI for discounted and SSP problems. The paper [Ber18d] describes the 
close relation of the operator T ($) µ with the proximal operator of convex 
analysis (see e.g., the author’s books [Ber15a] and [Ber16]), and establishes a close connection between temporal di!erence methods and the proximal algorithm. Variants of &-PI are described and analyzed in several works by Scherrer and his collaborators; see [Sch13], [EDS18], and the references quoted there. 
Another computational approach for exact infinite horizon DP is based on linear programming; see e.g., the textbooks [Ber12], [Ber19a], Section 5.6. Approximation methods based on linear programming, are not discussed in this book. They have been developed by de Farias and Van Roy [DFV03], [DFV04], [DeF04]. For a challenging application to pricing of network services, see Paschalidis and Tsitsiklis [PaT00]. For more recent work based on variants of the linear programming formulation, see Cogill et al. [CRV06], Desai, Farias, and Moallemi [DFM12], [DFM13], Wang, O’Donoghue, and Boyd [WOB15], Beuchat, Warring-ton, and Lygeros [BWL19], Banjac and Lygeros [BaL19], Tanzanakis and Lygeros [TaL20], and the references quoted there. 
Sections 5.3.3-5.3.4: The ideas of multiagent rollout and PI were introduced recently in the author’s paper [Ber19c], and further developed in the papers [Ber19d], [Ber20], [Ber21a]. Our definition of an agent-by-agent optimal policy is related to the notion of “person-by-person” optimality from team theory, which has been studied primarily in the context of multiagent decision problems. The notion of person-by-person optimality is also related to the notion of Nash optimality in multiperson games. The di!erence is that when the agents form a team, they have a common objective, while in multiperson Nash games the agents may have di!erent objectives. 
The research in team theory, generally assumes a nonclassical information pattern, whereby the agents may not share the information on
438 Infinite Horizon Problems Chap. 5 
which they base their decision. Thus team theory typically does not assume the shared information pattern that is characteristic of DP problems. As a result, there is no legitimate DP framework and associated Bellman’s equation, and the VI and PI methods are not valid anymore. For the origins of team theory and control with a nonclassical information pattern, we refer to Marschak [Mar55], Radner [Rad62], and Witsenhausen [Wit68], [Wit71a], [Wit71b]. A lot of research has followed the lead of these original works; see the references given for Section 3.2. 
Let us also note an alternative approach for team and multiagent problems, which is based on approximation in policy space, and applies to unconventional problem structures, including a nonclassical information pattern. Here, each agent has access to local observations, and the agent’s decision at each time is based on just the information available to him/her at that time. Despite the fact that DP does not directly apply, it is still possible to view multiagent control system design as a problem of parametric optimization, i.e., parametrize the policies of the agents and set up a framework for determining the parameters through some form of gradient optimization; see the RL textbook [Ber19a], Example 5.7.5. This is an approach with a long history in control methodology. For some recent applications and surveys of this approach to the multiagent control context, see the papers by Lowe et al. [LWT17], Hernandez-Leal, Kartal, and Taylor [HKT18], OroojlooyJadid and Hajinezhad [OrH19], Vinyals et al. [VBC19], Zhang, Yang, and Basar [ZYB19], and Nguyen, Nguyen, and Nahavandi [NNN20]. 
Sections 5.3.5-5.3.6: The stability of the on-line controller obtained by approximation in value space is of paramount importance in infinite horizon optimal control. This issue is discussed further in Exercises 5.1 and 5.2, which consider nonnegative cost deterministic problems (with arbitrary state and control spaces) and the role of sequential improvement conditions and multistep lookahead. 
Related stability issues are also important in adaptive control; see Ex-ercises 1.6, 3.2, and 5.3, which indicate that on-line approximation by value space tends to enhance the stability properties of the adaptive controller with respect to model uncertainties and parameter variations. 
Section 5.3.7: Q-learning and its variations is an important subject in RL, and has been researched extensively. A rigorous convergence proof of Q-learning was given by Tsitsiklis [Tsi94]. This proof combined several ideas from stochastic approximation theory and the theory of distributed asynchronous computation. It covered discounted problems, and SSP problems where all policies are proper. It also covered SSP problems with improper policies, assuming that the Q-learning iterates are either nonnegative or bounded. Convergence for SSP problems without the nonnegativity or the boundedness assumption was shown by Yu and Bertsekas [YuB13b]. Q-learning for optimal stopping problems was analyzed by Tsitsiklis and Van
Sec. 5.9 Notes and Sources 439 
Roy [TsV99], with followup work by Yu and Bertsekas [YuB07]. Optimistic asynchronous versions of PI based on Q-learning, which 
have solid convergence properties, are given by Bertsekas and Yu [BeY12], [YuB13a]. The distinctive feature of these methods is that the policy evaluation process aims towards the solution of an optimal stopping problem rather than towards the solution of the Bellman equation associated with the policy; this is needed to avoid the pathological behavior identified by Williams and Baird [WiB93], and noted in Section 5.8. 
The original proposal of SARSA is attributed to Rummery and Ni-ranjan [RuN94], with related work reported in the papers by Peng and Williams [PeW96], and Wiering and Schmidhuber [WiS98]. The ideas of the DQN algorithm attracted much attention following the paper by Mnih et al. [MKS15], which reported impressive test results on a suite of 49 classic Atari 2600 games. 
The principal di"culties in the application of DQN, is that it is primarily an o!-line algorithm, since it requires slow and complicated training. Moreover, even during o!-line training, it still has to deal with the issue of exploration. These di"culties are magnified when DQN is applied on-line, particularly in the context of on-line replanning and adaptive control. 
Exercise 5.6, based on the author’s recent paper [Ber21b], describes an approach to combine rollout and (exact or approximate) PI into a single on-line algorithm. The idea is to use the data accumulated from the rollout implementation to gradually improve the base policy, and to asymptotically obtain a policy that is either locally or globally optimal. The algorithm also o!ers the promise of interesting combinations with random search methods, Bayesian optimization, and approximations in value and policy space (see the relevant discussions in Section 3.5 and Chapter 4). 
In particular, we may represent the base policy of the rollout algorithm, either directly using approximation in policy space, or indirectly by using a value network that represents the policy’s Q-factors. As the system is operating on-line, new data in the form of (state, rollout control) pairs are generated. The data is then used to improve the quality of the policy through a suitable training algorithm. This type of scheme resembles somewhat the Q-learning and DQN algorithms, but it has the advantage that it is suitable for on-line replanning and adaptive control situations, since it is based on rollout, which is inherently an on-line algorithm, and is resilient to changes in the problem parameters. 
Section 5.4: The performance bounds of this section were given, together with their proofs, in the RL book [Ber19a], with the exception of the multiagent truncated rollout bound of Prop. 5.4.4, which is new. 
Section 5.5: The abstract DP framework is developed in great detail in the author’s monograph [Ber18a]. Earlier works on abstract DP include the (unweighted) contractive DP framework of Denardo [Den67], the author’s work on monotone increasing and monotone decreasing DP models [Ber77],
440 Infinite Horizon Problems Chap. 5 
and Chapters 2-6 of the book by Bertsekas and Shreve [BeS78]. Some of our abstract DP analysis is valid without requiring both 
the monotonicity and the contraction assumptions. In particular, the distributed asynchronous PI convergence results of Section 5.8 do not rely on the monotonicity assumption. For simplicity, we have not pursued this level of generality in this book, and we refer to the monograph [Ber18a] for a more refined analysis. 
Section 5.6: Multiagent VI was proposed in the author’s paper [Ber20]. The extension of the multiagent VI and PI methods to general abstract DP also comes from this source. The analysis of this section also highlights a conceptually important connection of rollout algorithms with coordinate descent methods, which optimize a problem’s variables one-at-a-time, while keeping the remaining variables fixed at their current values. 
Section 5.7: Asynchronous distributed VI methods were introduced by the author in the 1982 paper [Ber82]. The asynchronous convergence theorem and its application to DP and gradient optimization were first given by the author in the paper [Ber83]. The theorem has been applied extensively in the parallel and distributed computation book by Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis [BeT89] to a variety of contexts, including DP, gradient optimization, and others. For further applications of the theorem in DP, see the author’s books [Ber12], [Ber18a], [Ber19a]. 
Section 5.8: The distributed asynchronous optimistic PI algorithm with randomization of Section 5.8.1 was given in the monograph [Ber18a]. It has been suitably adapted to the context of the present work. A similar algorithm that is based on the &-PI method has been discussed by Li, Johansson, and Martensson [LJM19]. 
The distributed asynchronous PI methodology of Section 5.8.2 was developed in the papers by Bertsekas and Yu [BeY12], [YuB13a]. An earlier paper (Bertsekas and Yu [BeY10]) focuses on a simpler (nonoptimistic) version of asynchronous PI, which does not require the use of the mappings (5.88)-(5.90). The model of Exercise 5.10, which considers distributed asynchronous PI methods with feature-based cost function approximation, comes from the paper [BeY10]. The paper [BeY12] discusses also approximate implementations and provides an error bound for the case of discounted finite-state MDP. This error bound is very similar to the one of Prop. 5.4.5 for nonoptimistic PI. A related bound for optimistic PI, given in [Ber18a], Prop. 2.5.3. 
All these bounds are typically conservative, but provide some qualitative guidance for structuring the computations. In particular, it is shown that ultimately all these approximate PI methods (nonoptimistic, optimistic, and distributed asynchronous) oscillate within an error zone of size 
( + 2!* 
(1 # !)2 ,
Sec. 5.9 Notes and Sources 441 
where * and ( quantify the errors in the policy evaluation and policy improvement operations, respectively. This suggests that the methods are comparable in terms of performance error, which seems to be roughly consistent with practical experience. 
There is a dearth of experimental studies involving distributed PI algorithms with partitioned architectures at present. In fact the author knows of only one, by Bhatacharya et al. [BBW20], which involves a singleagent POMDP with as many as 1015 states, and as many as nine value and policy networks. Additional computational studies are needed, which involve more value and policy networks, and multiple agents. This will be significant, since parallelization is a major approach for mitigating the extreme computational requirements of large scale POMDP problems. 
We finally note that in our discussion of approximate PI in this book, we have not addressed several of the prominent approaches for approximate policy evaluation from the literature, such as temporal di!erence methods, as well as a variety of approximate Q-learning methods. These methods are important and are advertised widely, but they are not as well-suited for application of the parallelization ideas that we have focused on in this chapter. Interestingly they do not play a significant role in the AlphaZero program. Moreover, they are highly susceptible to the issues of exploration that were described at several points in this book, and are discussed at length in several of the RL textbooks. An important question in this regard is whether we can address more e!ectively the issue of adequate exploration with the state space partitioning approach that we have developed in this chapter. This is plausible, since by partitioning the state space, we may be able to target more equitably its parts for exploration.

5.6 (Simplified On-Line Policy Iteration - Combined Rollout and PI [Ber21b]) 
The purpose of this exercise is to introduce a version of the PI algorithm, where the policy improvement operation is done on-line and only for the states that are encountered during operation of the system. This is similar to Q-learning, but no cost function approximation is involved, and moreover full system trajectories are simulated to evaluate the cost function values of the current policy. 
The algorithm allows the combination of rollout with continuous updat-ing/improvement of the base policy, thus resulting in a form of on-line PI that incorporates the rollout controls into the current policy as new states and controls are generated. As discussed in Section 1.3, the rollout policy µ̃ corresponding to base policy µ can be interpreted in terms of a Newton iteration for solving the Bellman equation J! = TJ! starting from Jµ, and results in a superlinear convergence rate in the sense that 
)Jµ̃ ! J!) )Jµ ! J!) 
+ 0 as )Jµ ! J!) + 0. 
This suggests that the on-line PI algorithm of this exercise will also work very well compared with just using the base policy µ0. Moreover, in view of its rollout nature, the algorithm is well-suited for on-line replanning and adaptive control, where some of the problem parameters may change over time. 
We will focus primarily on convergence guarantees of our main on-line PI algorithm. In particular, we will show that it converges in a finite number of stages to a type of locally optimal policy [see part (b) below]. Possible extensions include the possibility of variants of PI and multiagent PI where the policy improvement is done by using random search methods. 
Further possibilities include on-line PI algorithms with various value and policy approximations, and exploration strategies (although this is not part of this exercise). Here, the base policy is represented either directly using approximation in policy space, or indirectly by using a value network that represents the policy’s Q-factors. New data in the form of (state, rollout control) pairs are generated during the on-line system operation, and is used to improve the current policy approximation using some training algorithm. Nonparametric methods (cf. Example 4.1.5) may be well-suited for this purpose. A Gaussian process representation of the cost function of the current policy (cf. Section 3.5) may also be useful.

Reinforcement Learning and Optimal Control Dimitri P. Bertsekas 
Athena Scientific, 2019 388 pp., hardcover, ISBN 978-1-886529-39-7 
This book explores the common boundary between optimal control and artificial intelligence, as it relates to reinforcement learning and simulation-based neural network methods. These are popular fields with many applications, which can provide approximate solutions to challenging sequential decision problems and large-scale dynamic programming (DP). The aim of the book is to organize coherently the broad mosaic of methods in these fields, which have a solid analytical and logical foundation, and have also proved successful in practice. 
The book discusses both approximation in value space and approximation in policy space. It adopts a gradual expository approach, which proceeds along four directions: 
 From exact DP to approximate DP: We first discuss exact DP algorithms, explain why they may be di!cult to implement, and then use them as the basis for approximations. 
 From finite horizon to infinite horizon problems: We first discuss finite horizon exact and approximate DP methodologies, which are intuitive and mathematically simple, and then progress to infinite horizon problems. 
 From model-based to model-free implementations: We first discuss model-based implementations, and then we identify schemes that can be appropriately modified to work with a simulator. 
The mathematical style of this book is somewhat di"erent from the one of the author’s DP books, and the 1996 neuro-dynamic programming (NDP) research monograph, written jointly with John Tsitsiklis. A rigorous, albeit short, mathematical account of the theory of finite and infinite horizon DP is provided, together with some fundamental approximation methods. However, the book relies more on intuitive explanations and less on proof-based insights. Moreover, the mathematical requirements are quite modest: calculus, a minimal use of matrix-vector algebra, and elementary probability. 
The book is supported by on-line video lectures and slides, as well as extensions and new research material, some of which has been covered in the present monograph.
